The matter must be brought to the attention of the Case Officer immediately so that a decision on recovery can be made.

<!-- Part1 p.226 -->

### Hearing evidence under oath

242. You have the statutory authority at an Inquiry to take evidence on oath or under an affirmation.

243. Hearing evidence on oath is most unlikely to be necessary at most s78 Inquiries, although it might occur where factual evidence is disputed. It is more common in Enforcement and similar Inquiries.

244. Further advice is provided in the Enforcement ITM Chapter and for advice on oaths at virtual / blended / Hybrid events, see ‘Advice on oaths at virtual and other Inquiries’.

### Requests to summons a witness

245. It may be that a representative of a body from which you wish to hear will not agree to attend the Inquiry. If this persists, following clear statements that attendance will be very helpful to you, which will often achieve the desired result, you have the power under s250(2) of the Local Government Act 1972 to issue a witness summons. It is a power that is used very rarely and should be exercised only as the very last resort. In any case, although you can compel someone to attend, you cannot require them to speak – so the exercise may be pointless. Seek advice from your IM or a PfL before using this power. For more information see Annex D.

### Should I hear any matters in private?

246. Section 321 of the 1990 Act requires that Inquiries are held in public, subject to very limited exceptions related to national security. Oral evidence shall be heard in public and documentary evidence shall be open to public inspection.

247. In such cases the Secretary of State can direct that the hearing of specific evidence be in private. If this suggestion arises, seek guidance from your IM or a PfL.

248. Commercial confidentiality or the privacy of individuals is not a sufficient justification for an in-camera session. Such requests must be rejected.

249. However it sometimes occurs that a party indicates that there is a personal matter which they need to discuss in private, as it could have an effect on how the inquiry progresses.

250. Inspectors must not have conversations with a single party, but it is important that you respond sensitively to this sort of occurrence. It might be that a witness (or an advocate) is unwell or has a personal issue (such as a bereavement) which they naturally do not want discussed in an open forum.

251. Under these circumstances you should invite the advocates for both parties (and any Rule 6 party) - perhaps with the person concerned if appropriate – to

<!-- Part1 p.227 -->

discuss the matter in your retiring room. It is impossible to be proscriptive about how you might resolve the issue – you will have to balance the need to progress the inquiry with the need to be sensitive to the particular issue.

252. When you resume the inquiry you should announce that you have a conversation with representatives of the main parties about a particular personal issue which has arisen. You have not been hearing evidence. You should not give any further explanation but announce any effect on the inquiry (especially related to timetabling).

253. All the above applies equally if you have a personal issue which requires a discussion with the parties.

### Should I allow filming and recording?

254. The presumption is that filming and recording will be allowed. You should ask in your opening if anyone intends to film or record the event. If so, check that everyone is comfortable with this (some may not, for example, wish to have their faces shown or voice recorded).

255. If there are concerns, you can ask that filming/recording is restricted to certain angles. It is never appropriate to film children or vulnerable adults even if no objections are raised. If filming/recording does take place, ask that it is carried out responsibly.

256. Inquiries may be live streamed (and therefore often automatically recorded). The LPA should normally arrange for the livestreaming, as they will usually be providing the venue (but there is no reason why the Appellant cannot do so). The livestreaming should generally be arranged either prior to or at the CMC, but increasing numbers of people or specific requests for livestreaming may change the position. If the Inquiry is to be livestreamed (and recorded), you should advise participants of this and ensure that the information is included in the Council’s notification letter to local residents if it is known at that stage

257. In circumstances where there are factors which outweigh the public interest in allowing the Inquiry to be filmed or recorded, it may be necessary for you to prevent or restrict it. If the venue has restrictions on filming in place, then confirmation will be needed before the Inquiry that those restrictions can be lifted.

258. If PINS receives a request to film or record beforehand, the Press Office or the Case Officer will inform you that this is being proposed.

### Video evidence

259. You may be asked to view video evidence (for example showing highway conditions or a virtual reality model of the proposed development). If so, you should make sure that all those at the Inquiry have had the opportunity to view

<!-- Part1 p.228 -->

and comment upon the recording, and that a witness will be available to explain the evidence and answer questions.

### High profile events

260. Some events will attract a significant number of interested parties, demonstrations and scrutiny by the press. It is essential that you refer to the Role of the Inspector chapter for full detail on how to deal with these circumstances.

261. It could be that either the appellant or the nature of the proposal, combined with press and social media interest, leads to exceptional levels of comment and potential risk.

262. The advice in the chapter referenced above is not repeated here, but it is essential that Inspectors discuss a potential issue with their IM and PfL at a very early stage – so that appropriate Risk Assessments and discussions with the Press Office can be undertaken.

### Audibility, linguistic or literacy difficulties

263. If there is no PA system and someone advises that they cannot hear the discussion, invite them to sit closer. Ask the parties to speak up and to look up when speaking. If it seems that audibility will be a continuing problem, for example, if there are large numbers of people present, consider a short so that microphones can be arranged.

264. If the livestream or Teams link goes down, you should immediately pause proceedings. Interested parties have been invited to a Public Inquiry, and whether they are listening or actively participating, it would be prejudicial to exclude them. In most cases the link can be restored rapidly, and when that happens you need to explain when you resume that the inquiry has not progressed in the meanwhile. If this takes longer you may have to adjourn until it can be restored.

265. ‘The venue and facilities for public Inquiries and hearings’ states that venues should have an installed and operational hearing loop and that a sign language interpreter should be arranged if necessary. These issues may be flagged up at the CMC or may arise on the day.

266. Some participants may not have a good understanding of English or may have poor literacy skills. See the advice in the Inspector Training Manual chapter on Human Rights and Equality. This may involve finding someone who can assist the participant.

### Requests for public funding

267. You might exceptionally be told that individuals are applying for legal aid (public

<!-- Part1 p.229 -->

funding) based on Article 6(1) of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, neither you nor the Secretary of State can entertain applications for public funding.

268. You should offer to assist those unfamiliar with Inquiry procedure as far as possible consistent with your role. It could also be suggested that the individuals might be able to co-operate with another party sharing part or all the same case; and that assistance may be available from Planning Aid, Citizens Advice, or other organisation offering free assistance or funding.

269. If a party decides to apply for public funding, it might very exceptionally be necessary to adjourn the Inquiry to give time for the application to be processed, although in a long Inquiry it may be possible to rearrange the programme to avoid an adjournment. See the Human Rights and Equality ITM Chapter for further advice.

### Procedures at a re-opened Inquiry

270. Although uncommon, there are various reasons why an Inquiry may be re-opened. This may include new evidence, new issues of fact or matters relating to natural justice. It may be at the request of the parties, the Secretary of State or at your own discretion. Consult your IM or a PfL if you have this in mind.

271. When new evidence or opinion is to be considered, the relevant witness(es) must attend the re-opened Inquiry to give their views on this evidence only.

272. When a new issue of fact has caused the Inquiry to be re-opened, the parties will have been told what it is, and they will be entitled to submit any evidence that reasonably bears upon it. It may not be necessary for anyone to attend and give evidence, although you can explain how you would like to proceed. If anyone does appear, this will be on the terms set out in the preceding paragraph.

273. When re-opening the Inquiry, you should emphasise that the proceedings are strictly limited to the consideration of the specific topic(s) or matter(s) requiring further examination.

274. Ideally, the re-opened Inquiry is taken by the original Inspector. If this is not possible, and it has fallen to you, you should prepare as you would for any other Inquiry, albeit the focus may be very narrow. Should you be faced with this discuss the position with your IM and/or PfL.

275. The usual procedure for your opening should be complied with. Before any representations are heard, you should explain the procedure to be adopted. If there are any procedural objections you should hear them and, if possible, resolve them by agreement. It may be relevant to consider what additional conditions, if any, might be imposed in relation to the matters discussed.

<!-- Part1 p.230 -->

276. The Rules regarding the previous submission of Rule 6 statements and proofs of evidence do not apply in a re-opened planning Inquiry. However, the Case Officer will normally have written to the parties to require statements and proofs. If this has not been done, you can set out a timetable for the receipt of evidence before the re-opening.

277. The body or person responsible for producing the new evidence or calling attention to the new issue should be asked to present their case first. The parties should then be heard in turn, followed by any interested persons11, with the Appellant being allowed the right of final reply. The Inquiry should then be closed.

### Voluntary re-opening

278. Powers are also available to you to enable an Inquiry to be re-opened voluntarily when not required by the Rules. Inquiries should only be re-opened voluntarily in highly exceptional circumstances (for example if an issue is likely to be of particular concern to interested persons) as the point at issue can usually be dealt with by written representations. If you consider that an Inquiry should be re-opened, you should consult your IM or a PfL.

### Re-determinations

279. An Inquiry may be re-opened for the re-determination of a case when a transferred or SoS decision has been quashed by the High Court, Appeal Court or Supreme Court.12 The quashed decision is treated as if it had not been made and is incapable of having had any legal effect. It is, however, capable of being a material consideration and, if so, you will need to explain in your decision/report any departures you may make from the previous reasoning.

280. Procedure at the re-opened Inquiry follows the normal sequence. In your opening announcement, you must make clear that you are re-opening the Inquiry held earlier and that the case must be re-determined as the previous decision was quashed by the court.

281. Because you must deal with the case afresh, all the original issues should be considered, as well as taking into account any new evidence or material changes since the first Inquiry (such as the emergence of new planning policies).

282. There may be scope for saving time in relation to matters unaffected by the court's decision, which were examined extensively previously and where

[^11]: Although you could deal with these first, to avoid them waiting around.

[^12]: Redetermined appeals can also be dealt with by means of a Hearing or by Written Representations. See s319A of the 1990 Act and Rule 20.

<!-- Part1 p.231 -->

nothing material has changed. Where this is the case, you should discuss this approach with the parties and seek their agreement. Make clear in your decision any areas where it has been agreed that it is unnecessary for further evidence to be given.

283. For more information, see ‘Redetermination following a High Court challenge’ in ‘The Approach to Decision Making’.

284. All re-determined appeal decisions/reports must be sent for pre-issue reading.

### Call-in applications and recovered appeals

285. Under s77 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 the Secretary of State may “call-in” planning applications for them to make the decision instead of the LPA. Inquiries into these applications are held under section 77. The Town and Country Planning (Inquiries Procedure) (England) Rules 2000 9SI 2000/1624) apply.

286. A call-in is enacted by a direction, which requires the planning application to be referred to the Secretary of State. The direction can only be given before the application is decided by the LPA, that is, before the decision notice has been issued. Call Ins normally relate to planning applications which raise issues of national significance.

287. Appeals are usually transferred to PINS for determination by an Inspector on behalf of the Secretary of State. However, the Secretary of State may also ‘recover’ the jurisdiction to decide an appeal (having regard to s79 of the Act). The appeal may be recovered at any stage before the decision is issued even after the Inquiry has taken place. The recovery letter will set out the reasons why the Secretary of State has recovered the decision.

288. In both cases, the Inspector will write a report to the Secretary of State which contains a recommendation on whether the application/appeal should be allowed or dismissed. The Secretary of State takes the report into account when making the decision. Further details are in the ITM chapter Secretary of State Casework

289. In both Call-In and Recovery cases the Secretary of State will have indicated those matters about which s/he particularly wishes to be informed. Especially in the former type of casework, this may be preliminary and will have been drafted before the submission of evidence. It is important that those aspects of the proposal which are not the subject of objection by the LPA are probed and reasoned for the benefit of the SoS – correspondence from interested parties may be a useful source of material for these matters. You should explain that you may be more inquisitorial than normal for this reason, but that this does not indicate bias. Additionally, you may allow more questioning from interested parties than would otherwise be the case. Each of the SoS’s matters, and other material considerations, need to be concluded upon.

<!-- Part1 p.232 -->

### Long Inquiries

### Programme Officers

290. A Programme Officer may be appointed to assist you in the administrative and procedural aspects of a long Inquiry, particularly one in which there are many participants. They can be of considerable benefit to you. If you feel that a Programme would be potentially helpful consult your IM and request one. A good Programme Officer can save time at the event and relieve some of the administrative burden on the Case Officer and the Inspector beforehand.

291. The Programme Officer must be accepted and recognised by all as an officer of the Inquiry responsible to and under the sole direction of you. During the pre-Inquiry period, and throughout the Inquiry itself, the Programme Officer must be, and must be seen to be, completely impartial. It is essential that the Programme Officer can deal directly with the public.

292. You should make these points at the CMC and at the opening of the Inquiry. It is very useful for a programme Officer to be appointed as soon as possible so they can attend the CMC.

293. It is normally the case that a Programme Officer is appointed by the LPA. There are many independent Programme Officers, or the LPA may provide an officer unconnected with the proposal. If the appointed Programme Officer is unfamiliar with the role, as may well be the case with an LPA officer, it is essential that the Inspector contacts them at an early stage to agree the role and expectations.

294. The Programme Officer could be responsible for:

- organising the Inquiry programme, dealing with procedural queries relating to the programme and managing event logistics (including room set up and day-to-day queries from attendees).

- providing a link between you and the participants.

- facilitating site visits, whether accompanied or otherwise.

- receiving and distributing all Inquiry documents and ensuring that all documents received before and during the Inquiry are available in an up-to-date online Inquiry library.

295. The Programme Officer should be provided with an office outside the Inquiry room. Their contact details will need to be available to all those with an interest in the appeal.

<!-- Part1 p.233 -->

### Inspector Panels

296. Occasionally, a case may require a panel of Inspectors. This will be due to the length or complexity of the case being determined; recent examples are the Bristol and Luton Airport appeals and the Cambridge Guided Busway. There will always need to be a Lead Inspector, although just the term ‘Inspector’ should be used on a daily basis. The role of each Inspector is to work on aspects of the appeal both before, during and after the Inquiry and to write part of the decision/report. The overall report and conclusions/recommendations should be jointly agreed.

297. It is for the Inspectors to agree what tasks each panel member undertakes, under the guidance of the Lead Inspector. Each Inspector may:

- Read the evidence on particular topics, including supporting evidence, and prepare any questions on those topics.

- Conduct sessions of the Inquiry on specific topics.

- Draft parts of the report, including (but not exclusively) sections on particular topics where they conducted the Inquiry session.

298. All the Inspectors should, if possible, attend the CMC and all sessions of the Inquiry and any site visits. In the event of an Inspector becoming ill after the Inquiry has been opened, it may be possible for the Inquiry and decision/report to proceed if this is appropriate. In that way the need to re-start or re-open the Inquiry would be avoided.

### Appeal Planning Officer

299. If you are provided with the assistance of one of our APOs, they will have been selected to assist you in administrative tasks and can help with things like summarising representations or reports. They do not need to join you at any part of the event/CMC, unless this has been agreed as a development opportunity for them, but if they do you should briefly introduce them and explain their functions. It should be made clear that they have no part in the decision making process and that any recommendations / conclusions in your report / decision remain yours.

### Evening sessions

300. Evening sessions may occasionally be necessary when there are a high number of interested parties who wish to speak, and/or if there are a high number of potential attendees who are not free during the day. Virtual participation may reduce the need for/length of evening sessions.

<!-- Part1 p.234 -->

301. You should seek the agreement of the main parties well in advance, to ensure that they are able to accommodate the evening session, given potential domestic commitments or logistical issues.

302. Evening sessions can be beneficial in facilitating public access to the event, but must not result in an excessively long day for anyone – including the Inspector. The main session should adjourn by early/mid afternoon, to enable everyone to take a decent break.

303. An evening session needs to be arranged and controlled carefully. You must make it clear that it is part of the Inquiry and not a public meeting. All speakers must observe the normal Inquiry rules, addressing you rather than the public at large and not repeating points already made (although be mindful that speakers may be inexperienced and be nervous). All attendees should be respectful, refraining from commenting, clapping or cheering.

304. If possible, the Programme Officer or an LPA representative should collect in advance a list of those wishing to speak, together with a brief outline of the points they wish to make. You should hear first from those who have requested to speak, before asking if any other attendees wish to speak.

### Controlling the pace of a long Inquiry

305. You need to set a reasonable pace, as Inquiries that go on for many weeks are tiring for all concerned. Especially for those who have to travel long distances.

306. You should ensure that you have adequate time for preparation; your programme immediately before the event should not include cases of significant size. All outstanding work should be completed before a long inquiry begins – otherwise timeliness will suffer and it will be hard to get back to an earlier case when you emerge from a long inquiry.

307. The Inquiry programme should be based on a programme running from Tuesday to Thursday and a half day on a Friday, or simply Tuesday to Thursday if your own or the parties’ travel distance is considerable.

308. Be realistic when estimating how long the various stages of the Inquiry will take and understand that there will be considerable amounts of work taking place ‘behind the scenes’ by the main parties, who may need time to address matters between themselves. You may also need time to catch up and/or prepare for subsequent sessions.

309. You may find that an adjournment of a week part way through a multi-week Inquiry is beneficial to allow you and the parties time to consolidate the outcomes of the previous weeks. This possibility should be flagged up at the CMC and incorporated into the programme - this is not wasted time and would

<!-- Part1 p.235 -->

be unlikely to delay the decision/report as you can be working on the first stage(s) of the inquiry in the gap.

310. Inspector Managers facing a long Inquiry should ask a fellow IM to deal with day-to-day queries from members of their groups.

### Joint Inquiries and non-planning cases

311. Some joint Inquiries are difficult to programme. An example is a joint Inquiry into an application for planning permission and a CPO relating to the same site, where the relevant procedural rules cannot be followed strictly.

312. When considering the programme of an Inquiry other than a s78 case, it should be remembered that the party that is asking the Secretary of State to do something should normally go first and end last. Thus, if the subject of the Inquiry is the confirmation of a CPO, the order making authority should go first.

313. If the Secretary of State is making a proposal, such as a modification or revocation order, their representative should make their statement first.

314. You should declare at the outset what variant of the Rules should be applied and ask the main parties to consent to it. The procedures customarily followed in Inquiries under the Highways Acts should not, however, be used in other types of case. If you are in doubt about the best and fairest procedure, first seek advice from your IM of IPL, and seek the parties agreement.

<!-- Part1 p.236 -->

### Annex C: Content And Format of Proofs and Appendices

(Edit as required for personal preference)

### Content

Proofs of evidence must:

- refer to the information that witnesses wish the Inspector to consider;

- cover only areas which remain at issue between the parties;

- contain the witness’s concisely expressed opinion;

- contain a clear cross reference to any supporting documents in the CD library

- Be page and paragraph numbered

Proofs must not:

- duplicate information already included in other Inquiry material, such as site description, planning history and relevant planning policy (usually in the SOCG(s);

- include new evidence;

- include extensive appendices – these should be in the CD library

- include long irrelevant biographical detail of the witness.

### Format of the proofs and appendices:

- Proofs to be no longer than 3,000 words if possible and where proofs are longer than 1,500 words, summaries are to be submitted. They must not introduce new or different evidence nor go beyond the scope of the text they summarise.

- Front covers to proofs and appendices are to be clearly titled, with the name, job title and qualifications of the witness on the cover.

- If paper copies are provided, proofs are to be spiral bound or bound in such a way as to be easily opened and read. Any appendices are to be bound separately and indexed using projecting tabs, labelled and paginated.

### Annex E: Assessors at Inquiries

### The status of an Assessor

1. An Assessor (as defined under Rule 2(1)) is a specialist adviser, usually scientific or technical, selected to assist you by hearing, testing and weighing evidence of a specialised nature that may be outside your normal experience, but which may have a bearing on the issues to be decided.

2. Assessors are appointed by the Secretary of State for a particular Inquiry and should hold a letter to that effect in case their status is challenged. In planning cases the Assessor's name and qualifications will be notified to the parties together with the matters on which the Inspector is to be advised. An Assessor may be a suitably qualified / experienced Planning Inspector or a third party.

3. It is important that Assessors should not have had any previous connection with the appeal proposal nor any professional association nor connection with the parties. Where the number of experts in the relevant field is so small that these conditions cannot be met it is essential that a statement of the position is made at the beginning of the Inquiry.

4. It is also important that the Assessor should not have taken a public stance on the policies or matters at issue in the Inquiry.

5. If Assessors realise, after accepting the appointment, that they have had some previous connection with the case or the parties, or if any other situation arises in which they might find their position gives rise to a perception of bias, they should immediately advise the Inspector.

6. Once an appointment as an Assessor has been offered there should be no private communication by them with the parties or with any interested person. If the Assessor considers that further information should be obtained from any of the parties before the Inquiry, they should, after discussion with the Inspector, ask the Case Officer to obtain it.

### Function of an Assessor

7. The Assessor's task is to evaluate the specialist evidence within their field that is presented at the Inquiry and to indicate the weight which it should, in their opinion, be given in your conclusions. It is the Assessor’s responsibility to ensure that, as far as possible, all relevant evidence within their specialised field is considered.

### Before the Inquiry

8. Assessors are sent copies of the Inquiry papers as soon as possible after accepting the appointment. They are also notified of the name of the

<!-- Part1 p.250 -->

Inspector. It is important that you and the Assessor discuss the case at an early stage. It will be very useful for the Assessor to attend the CMC.

9. Matters which might be discussed before the CMC or the Inquiry include:

- the precise boundaries of the Assessor's specialist interest in relation to the subject matter of the Inquiry and the extent to which they will be involved in asking questions at the event itself;

- the definition of issues and topics on which evidence will be needed; the adequacy of the specialist evidence coming forward; whether further information should be obtained from the parties; whether it appears that a witness does not intend to consider a key document (for example a published technical report) known to the Assessor; and whether there are any serious inconsistencies which the parties could be asked to clear up before the Inquiry. Such matters may form the basis for advice to the parties;

- points of procedure on which the Assessor requires clarification, including points arising from this advice;

- the programming of the Inquiry with reference to the specialist content and whether it is necessary for the Assessor to attend all sessions;

- how the Assessor sees the specialist issues standing at the beginning of the Inquiry and the aspects which need to be pursued.

10. The full statements of case, SOCGs and Proofs should be sent to the Assessor. The Assessor must arrange adequate preparation time before the Inquiry so that points of clarification and follow-up questioning can be identified. Inquiry

### Accompanied site visit (if necessary)

11. The assessor should normally attend the site visit. The Assessor and the Inspector should keep close together throughout the visit, because if something is pointed out to one, the other should also be aware of it.

### The report or decision

12. The Assessor will give advice to the Inspector on the specialist issues and will collaborate in the production of the report or decision. It is for the Inspector to ascertain the facts, however, and to reach their own conclusions.

<!-- Part1 p.251 -->

13. Where the specialist issues are complicated or difficult, the Assessor may assist you by preparing draft findings on those issues and any conclusions to be drawn from them which you may adopt. It must be clearly understood that they become your findings and conclusions, and you must accept full responsibility for them. Any draft conclusions of the Assessor's should derive from what has been seen and heard at the Inquiry.

14. Assessors' conclusions will be arrived at in the light of their specialist knowledge and experience and a background of generally accepted data on such matters can be assumed. The Assessor should not, however, take into account any new or controversial technical material which has not been considered at the Inquiry.

15. In many cases, all that will be necessary is for you to state at the end of your conclusions, "The Assessor, [Mr/Ms/Mx] .......... agrees with my conclusions in paragraphs ......" provided that is so.

16. Alternatively, if it is felt that the Assessor's contribution should be more clearly identified, it should be possible to frame the report in such a way that the specialist advice can be introduced in appropriate places by the phrase "I am advised by the Assessor that ....".

17. In cases where there has been a great deal of argument and where the decision turns on specialist issues, it may be appropriate for the Assessor to produce a written report to you. In a Secretary of State case, this is appended to your own report and you state how far it is accepted. In a standard case, it is not normally appended to the decision but a reference to its existence is made and it is made available for inspection.

18. If a report is produced, it must bear the Assessor's signature. It should carry the appropriate file reference and be headed by the appropriate brief title, such as "Compulsory Purchase Order ......" and the suffix "Assessor's Report".

### Annex G - Requests for a witness summons

1. You have the power under Section 250(2) of the Local Government Act 1972 to issue a witness summons. It is a power that is used very rarely and should be exercised with extreme caution and only as the very last resort. A blank witness summons form can be found in Annex 2 of the Enforcement ITM Chapter.

2. Parties applying for a summons should be made fully aware that they are required to pay out-of-pocket expenses, including compensation for loss of earnings where appropriate, to the witness they want to be summonsed. The party who applied for it must serve the summons and they are liable for any costs involved. If these responsibilities are accepted, you must then consider the case for issuing the summons.

3. Before issuing a summons you must be reasonably satisfied that:

- the evidence to be given by the witness is likely to be material to the case.

- the witness is the appropriate person to give the evidence.

- the witness will not come unless a summons is served.

- the production of an affidavit would not obviate the need for personal attendance.

4. If you exceptionally decide that a summons ought to be issued, the proceedings may have to be adjourned (to a fixed date) because the summons must be drawn up and be signed by you personally. An alternative is to continue with the Inquiry, hearing other evidence until the date on which summoned witnesses are required to attend.

5. In either case, you will need to know the name and address of the person requesting the summons, the name and address of the person summoned (the witness) and what documents, if any, the witness may be asked to produce. You need to get written confirmation from the person requesting the summons that they are prepared to meet all justifiable costs.

6. You may, very exceptionally, find it necessary to issue a witness summons of your own volition to elicit information which has not been forthcoming from the case as presented by the parties and where the parties have declined your invitation to adduce further evidence. You should bear in mind that PINS will have to pay expenses to the witness. You should consult a PfL before embarking on this course.

7. If a witness fails to appear in response to a summons, the Inquiry must be continued and the non-appearance reported to the office. The party who

<!-- Part1 p.255 -->

requested the summons may commence legal proceedings. It should be noted that if a witness does appear, and refuses to give evidence, he or she may be liable on summary conviction to a fine or imprisonment.

<!-- Part1 p.256 -->

### Annex I: Example s78 Inquiry Opening

To be adapted as appropriate.

Consider use of bullet points only – can sound better than reading from a script.

### Introduction

### Annex J - Absence of a main party (irresponsible behaviour)

1 Section 79(6A) of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 gives the Secretary of State the authority, after issuing a warning notice, to dismiss an appeal if the appellant is responsible for undue delay in its progress. It is intended that this power should only be used where an appellant/agent refuses to co-operate in processing the appeal or obstructs that process. Consult your IM or a PfL is this is in your mind.

2 “Undue delay” is most likely to occur due to the appellant or their representative’s failure to attend arranged site visits or events without providing a satisfactory reason but it also applies when the appellant does not complete necessary procedural steps (such as clarifying which conditions are being appealed or undertaking any statutory notifications) which prevents the Inspector from progressing with the determination of the appeal

3 If you have reason to believe that the appellant is behaving irresponsibly and has caused/is causing an undue delay in the process, the case of the LPA and those of any other parties present at an Inquiry may still be heard, along with any applications for costs. Where it is possible to make an unaccompanied site visit the Inquiry should be closed. On such a visit particular care should be taken not to get into conversation with any person near or at the site or to trespass on private property.

4 If it is clear from your pre-Inquiry site visit that an accompanied site visit is necessary, and it has not been possible to carry one out during the course of the Inquiry, agree a time and date with the LPA and any other parties who wish to be present at the site visit. The date should be 2 to 3 weeks ahead to allow time for contact to be made with the absent party. The Inquiry should then be closed.

5 You should contact the Case Officer with the relevant site visit details and inform them that you wish to invoke the process under section 79(6A). The Case Officer will write to the parties telling them of the date and time that you will attend to visit the site. The letter will also draw the absent party’s attention to s79(6A) of the Town and County Planning Act 1990 as amended by s18 of the Planning and Compensation Act 1991. This applies to all appeals made under s78 (and s174), regardless of procedure or site visit type, and states:

“If at any time before or during the determination of such an appeal it appears to the Secretary of State that the appellant is responsible for undue delay in the progress of the appeal, he may

a) give the appellant notice that the appeal will be dismissed unless the appellant takes, within the period specified in the notice, steps as are specified in the notice for the expedition of the appeal; and

<!-- Part1 p.265 -->

b) if the appellant fails to take those steps within that period, dismiss the appeal accordingly.

6 If the Appellant fails to turn up to the subsequent site visit or fails to allow the Inspector onto the site, the visit should be aborted and the Case Officer notified so that the appropriate letters can be issued dismissing the appeal. In that event, any correspondence about costs that pre-dates the site visit should be considered by the Costs Team.

7 The Case Officer has access to the suite of letters needed to complete the process before the appeal can be finally dismissed. The Inspector may need to provide some wording for the letters on a case-by-case basis.

8 This also applies to enforcement appeal and similar cases. In such cases, you will first determine whether the Appellant has acted responsibly or irresponsibly. After closing the Inquiry, if it is necessary to enter the site, arrange to meet the parties at the site and see if the Appellant or anyone else with authority to allow entry is there and will let you in (although s324 of the1990 Act does provide for rights of entry).

9 If you and other parties are let in the site visit can take place. If not, abort the visit, inform the Case Officer, who will write to the Appellant inviting further representations on the issue and highlighting any costs application. You will then determine the appeal based on the evidence before you.

10 If the Appellant has not allowed entry to check vital measurements, they may have failed to satisfy you, on the balance of probability, that their own asserted measurements (if any) are correct and accordingly has failed to discharge the onus of proof which is on them to demonstrate that the development is lawful and the appeal may be dismissed with or without costs.

11 Where an application for costs is made you will prepare a report for Cost Team who will complete the process.

### Annex K: Managing Disruptive Parties

As a responsible employer PINS has a duty of care to its staff. Our Customer Charter states that we expect all staff to be treated with courtesy and respect and warns that we will not tolerate rude or abusive behaviour. All staff are entitled to carry out their duties without fear of abuse or harassment.

The purpose of this note is to advise on the steps to follow when action is required.

### Powers

1. Rule 16 (9) of the Town and Country Planning (Inquiries Procedure) (England) Rules 200013 and Rule 11 (8) of the Town and Country Planning (Hearings Procedure) (England) Rules 200014 empower Inspectors to require participants at Hearings and Inquiries to leave if they are being disruptive15.

2. The Inspector may refuse to allow the person who has been asked to leave to return or permit a return only on such conditions that the Inspector may specify. Rule 15 (11) and Rule 11 (10) allow the Inspector to proceed in the absence of any person entitled to appear at the event.

### What is unreasonable/unacceptable behaviour?

3. Unreasonable/unacceptable behaviour is anything which disrupts the smooth running of the Inquiry, prevents you from focusing on the arguments or prevents any party from making their case. This could range from threats or shows of aggression to constant low-level interruptions. This may exhibit itself as bullying or belittling a witness or an opposing barrister.

4. Filming and recording of events should be allowed. If, however, you consider the way this is happening is intimidating you should ask that it stops. If the person recording refuses, this constitutes unreasonable behaviour.

### What to do about unreasonable/unacceptable behaviour?

5. Your training will have equipped you to deal with most situations. In short, if a party’s behaviour becomes disruptive, explain:

[^13]: Rule 16 (9) of The Town and Country Planning Appeals (Determination by Inspectors) (Inquiries Procedure) (England) Rules 2000 No 1625, or Rule 18 (9) of the Town and Country Planning (Enforcement) (Inquiries Procedure) (England) Rules 2002 No 2686, or Rule 17 (9) of the Town and Country Planning (Enforcement) (Determination by Inspectors) (Inquiries Procedure) (England) Rules 2002 No 2685 Rights of Way: Rule 9(9) of the Rights of Way (Hearings and Inquiries Procedure) (England) Rules 2007 Also Rule 11 (8) of the Town and Country Planning (Enforcement) (Hearings Procedure) (England) Rules 2002 No 2684 NSIP: Section 95 of the Planning Act 2008

[^15]: Any person required to leave may submit any evidence or other matter in writing before the close of the Hearing or Inquiry

<!-- Part1 p.267 -->

i. why their behaviour is unreasonable and that if they continue you will adjourn to give them time to calm down/reflect. If necessary/appropriate you could set conditions for their return (see Rules 15 and 11 above). Explain that if you are forced to adjourn because of their unreasonable behaviour you have the power to instigate an award of costs against them.

ii. that if they continue to behave unreasonably you will invoke your powers under Rule 15 (11) 16 or Rule 11 (10) and have them removed.

iii. that if they are removed, they may submit any evidence or other matter in writing before the close of the Inquiry.

6. All the above needs to be properly documented in order that any subsequent complaint or challenge may be addressed. If a party refuses to leave, adjourn and request that the Council’s security accompanies the disruptive person from the premises. If that is not possible, or in the event of serious disruptive behaviour or threat activate, your lone worker protection alarm (ORBIS) or call 99917.

## Legislation and Guidance

- The Town and Country Planning Act 1990 (as amended) – ‘the 1990 Act’

- The Town and Country Planning (Appeals) (Written Representations Procedure) (England) (Amendment and Saving Provisions) Regulations 2026 – ‘the 2026 Regs’

- Town and Country Planning (Appeals) (Written Representations Procedure) (England) Regulations 2009 (SI 2009/452), as amended – ‘the 2009 Regs’

- Town and Country Planning (Development Management Procedure) (England) Order 2015 (SI 2015/595), as amended – ‘the 2015 Order’

- Procedural Guide – Planning Appeals – England - Post 1st April 20261.

## Introduction

1. The Town and Country Planning (Appeals) (Written Representations Procedure) (England) Regulations 2009 (Statutory Instrument 2009/452) (as amended) provides for two different written representations procedures for appeals made under section 78(1) and 78(2) of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 (as amended) against a decision by a local planning authority to refuse a planning application, a failure to determine the application within the timeframe or against any conditions imposed with a grant of planning permission. These fall under Part 1 and Part 2.

2. The changes introduced by the 2026 Regulations will apply to appeals submitted under section 78(1) of the 1990 Act in relation to planning applications made on or after 1 April 2026. They also apply to appeals submitted under section 78(1) of the 1990 Act as modified by regulations made under section 220 of the 1990 Act in relation to applications for advertisement consent made on or after 1 April 2026.

3. Appeals relating to applications made before this date will continue under existing procedures. The Procedural Guide has been updated to reflect this.

4. All householder appeals, minor commercial appeals and applications for advertisement consent appeals submitted after the coming into force date will follow same Part 1 process as other written representations appeals. The only exception being the timescales for submission of these appeals which remain unchanged.

[^1]: The Procedural Guide – Planning appeals – England has been developed in two parts to account for the transition period. The original Guide (pre 31st March 2026) applies to planning appeals, householder development appeals, minor commercial appeals, listed building appeals, advertisement appeals and discontinuance notice appeals.

<!-- Part1 p.273 -->

5. This chapter will only cover appeals submitted under Part 1 for the time being, until a new chapter is developed.

6. It is expected that most written representation appeals will proceed under Part 1, which is an expedited procedure. The statutory instrument, the 2026 Regulations, amends the existing Part 1 process by expanding the scope of Part 1 to include all written representation appeals made under section 78(1) of the 1990 Act. However, the legislation also gives PINS the discretion to progress s78 appeals under Part 2, Hearing or Inquiry, where we deem it appropriate to do so.

7. The amended statutory instrument also limits what information can be submitted at the point of making the appeal via amendments to Article 37 (3) (a) of the 2015 Order.

8. Appeals under Part 1 are determined on the same basis as the original planning application. The appellant can submit limited reasons for appealing, but this should not add any new material or evidence, and the LPA will have the option to raise factual inaccuracies with those. The LPA will also provide the plans upon which it made its decision, along with all representations it received during the application process.

9. There is no opportunity for any interested parties to submit any representations during the appeal, but all representations submitted during the application phase will form part of the appeal, unless they are withdrawn. The LPA will cover this in their Notification Letter.

## The scope of Part 1 Appeals

10. The cases which fall within the scope of Part 1 are set out in the 2026 Regulations, the 2015 Order and in the Procedural Guide.

11. With few exceptions (see para 12/13 below) all s78(1) appeals will follow the Part 1 process in the first instance. These are appeals against:

- Refusal of planning permission;

- Grant of planning permission subject to conditions to which the applicant objects;

- Refusal of prior approval;

- Refusal of advertisement consent;

- Refusal of an application to approve a reserved matter;

- Refusal of an application to modify or remove a condition under section 73 of the 1990 Act;

<!-- Part1 p.274 -->

- Refusal of an application for planning permission for development already carried out under section 73A of the 1990 Act; and

- Refusal of Permission in Principle or Technical Details Consent.

12. The following section 78(1) appeals will not usually follow the Part 1 process after initial screening:

- Appeals proceeding as Hearings or Inquiries;

- Appeals against Biodiversity Net Gain Plans because of the requirements of article 37E of the 2015 Order; and

- Redetermination appeals. These may follow a different process so the relevant PfL will decide which process it will follow. It may be possible for the appeal to remain in Part 1.

13. Appeals that will not follow the Part 1 process because they are not made under section 78(1) of the 1990 act include:

- Appeals against non-determination (failure cases);

- Appeals made under directions given under section 77 of the 1990 Act (call-in cases);

- Appeals made under section 20 of the Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990 for listed building consent (Y appeals);

- Tree Preservation Order appeals, Hedgerow removal and High Hedge appeals;

- Appeals following the service of an enforcement notice (C appeals);

- Appeals relating to certificates of lawful development or use (X appeals); and

- Modification of section 106 agreements (Q appeals).

## The Part 1 appeal process

14. The appeal process is set out in the 2026 Regulations and, in summary, is as follows:

### Process | Timescale

Appeal made | Advertisement – within 8 weeks of the LPA decision Householder – within 12 weeks of LPA decisions Minor commercial – within 12 weeks of the LPA decision And all other appeal types within 6 months of the LPA decision

<!-- Part1 p.275 -->

Appellant’s Reasons for Appeal ‘Reasons for Appeal’ are not required but PINS has the power to ask for them within the appeal form.

PINS confirm appeal suitable As soon as practicable upon receipt of a valid appeal for Part 1 (the start date).

LPA provides questionnaire | Within 5 working days of the start date of the appeal and all documents and plans the LPA considered in their determination LPA tells interested people | Within 5 working days of the start date of the appeal about the appeal

Inspector visits the site | Between 2 and 6 weeks after the start date

Inspector makes decision | Decision issued as soon as practicable after the SV is complete.

### Appeal documents and evidence

15. All the appeal documents should be available on the Manage Appeals system but if you think a document is missing contact the Case Officer.

16. The Part 1 process is based on the assumption that a decision can reasonably be made on the basis of:

- The plans which were before the LPA when it made its decision – this includes any revisions made during the application process. If there is any doubt about the correct plans – ask the Case Officer to seek clarification from the parties;

- The LPA’s case as set out in the reasons for refusal and in any officer/committee report/minutes;

- The appellant’s reasons for appealing;

- Interested party representations made in connection with the application; and

- Any other relevant documents provided with the LPA questionnaire.

17. The Part 1 process does not allow any opportunity for:

- the LPA to comment on the appellant’s reasons for appealing, other than to set out factual errors therein, the assumption being that the LPA’s case should be clearly and adequately documented at the time their decision was made – even if the decision has been made contrary to the officer’s

<!-- Part1 p.276 -->

recommendation, whether through the Officer’s Report or a member overturn/elected members/planning committee;

- Interested parties to make any additional comments during the appeal process; or

- Amended plans or documents to be submitted.

18. However, Regulation 8 of the 2009 Regs does allow you to request further information relevant to the appeal. Regulation 8 allows that:

- ‘The Secretary of State may in writing require the appellant, local planning authority and other interested persons, to provide such further information relevant to the appeal as may be specified.’

19. The LPA will notify interested parties of the appeal and offer them the option, by writing to PINS, of withdrawing any representations made in response to the planning application.

### What must the appellant submit with the appeal?

20. A copy of the original application form, the appeal form (containing their reasons for appealing), and the LPA decision notice

21. The appellant’s reasons for appealing should provide a concise summary of why they believe the LPA’s decision should be overturned. It should not introduce new evidence, extra material, technical evidence or arguments not previously put to the LPA at the application stage.

22. Amended drawings and/ or documents will not be accepted and the appeal form does not allow for their submission. The appellant would need to reapply to the LPA.

### What must the LPA submit?

23. The LPA will be responsible for submitting all the documentation considered at application stage and a copy of all the relevant plans and reports it based its decision on Additionally, LPAs will be encouraged to set this information out within the decision notice so as to minimise disputes as to the relevant documentation.

24. If the decision is a member/committee overturn then the LPA should ensure that committee minutes are sufficiently detailed. You should rely on the committee minutes and the reasons for refusal as the LPA’s case.

25. The LPA can only respond to the Appellant’s reasons for appealing by identifying any factual errors in that documentation. It may also explain any change in circumstances that have occurred since the decision was made such as a new local plan, national policy changes, changes to the housing land supply position.

<!-- Part1 p.277 -->

## Transferring cases out of Part 1 into Part 2

26. Regulation 9 of the 2009 Regs allows the Secretary of State, thus PINS, to determine that an appeal is not suitable for Part 1 and should be dealt with under Part 2. Cases will only be moved to Part 2 in exceptional circumstances and you must discuss this with your Manager in the first instance before a transfer decision is made.

27. Examples of cases that will not be suitable for Part 1 include where:

- The case falls outside the scope of Part 1 (see here);

- The case raises more complex issues that require the parties to make extensive representations or would require an oral event to enable a full exploration of the issues at hand; or

- The appeal should be linked with another related appeal, though not another s78; for example, an enforcement or listed building appeal.

28. A change in circumstances does not automatically justify a move to Part 2. In many cases, changes can be addressed by inviting comments under Regulation 8 of the 2009 Regs which allows that:

- ‘The Secretary of State may in writing require the appellant, local planning authority and other interested persons, to provide such further information relevant to the appeal as may be specified.’

29. Consequently, it may be appropriate to seek the views of the parties if the issue is a straightforward one and it would be reasonable to require comments to be made within a restricted time period (for example, 5 days) - this might include cases where it is necessary to seek clarification about a newly adopted development plan policy or to seek comments about the potential imposition of a non-standard condition. A template for the wording you must use is at Annex 1.

30. Case Officers will look to see if the parties have provided any evidence which might mean the case should be taken out of Part 1 or invalidated. However, responsibility rests with you, so you need to make sure the principles of natural justice are adhered to. You should not take into account evidence which any party (such as the appellant, LPA and/or neighbours) would not have been aware of and ought to have been given the opportunity to comment upon. This is most likely to involve technical evidence such as a biodiversity survey, traffic or flood report for example.

31. Ultimately, whether you are initially reviewing the case or preparing for the site visit, you should consider whether there might be any reasons that require the appeal to be transferred out of Part 1.

32. If it is agreed with your Manager that, exceptionally, a case should be taken out of Part 1 you should contact the Case Officer and Case Team Leader as soon as

<!-- Part1 p.278 -->

possible and provide some explanation for the letter to the parties. The case will need to be transferred from Part 1 to Part 2 and it will be necessary to restart the appeal as the appeal timetable will need to be revised to accommodate the appellant’s full statement of case, comments from interested parties, and the local planning authority’s statement.

### What happens if I need to undertake a HRA and need more information?

33. Part 1 does not remove any requirements or process that are required under the Habitats Regulations (2017) (as amended). Further guidance can be found in the ITM Natural Environment chapter and if you are unsure on seeking more information, this should be discussed with your Manager.

34. Under the 2009 Regs, Regulation 8 allows for an Inspector to require the appellant, LPA and other statutory or interested persons, to provide further information relevant to the appeal. This information must be provided in writing, and you should ensure you set clear deadlines to avoid the decision being delayed. A template for the wording you must use is at Annex 1.

35. When submitting a request under Regulation 8, Inspectors should also complete the Regulation 8 Feedback Form to support monitoring of consistency, effectiveness of the Part 1 process, and potential areas for external engagement to help reduce delays.

36. If you require further information under Regulation 8, you must consider whether the nature of the information sought interferes with the principles of natural justice and would, therefore, require it to be shared with interested parties for comment, and opportunities given to the appellant/LPA to comment on any responses. If this is the case, it may need to be transferred to Part 2.

### What happens if an Environmental Statement is required?

37. If an ES was submitted at application stage, and has been appropriately consulted upon already, the appeal can stay in Part 1.

38. The appeal would only need to move to Part 2, if it is subsequently deemed that an ES is required.

### What if I need further information to discharge the PSED or where Article 8 or other Human Rights may be engaged?

39. The appeal can stay in Part 1, if nature of the information is straight forward. It could move to Part 2 if it requires additional consultation and representations to be made or where the evidence needs to be tested or explored further at a Hearing or Inquiry

40. Regulation 8 allows for an Inspector to require the appellant, LPA and other statutory or interested persons, to provide further information relevant to the appeal. This information must be provided in writing, and you should ensure you

<!-- Part1 p.279 -->

set clear deadlines to avoid the decision being delayed. A template for the wording you must use is at Annex 1.

## Safeguarding

41. Are there any safeguarding issues? If you have any safeguarding concerns, advice is contained in the Approach to Decision Making chapter

## Site visits

42. There are two types of site visit in Part 1 casework and you should read the ITM chapter on Site Visits for full information but as a summary:

Unaccompanied site visits (USV)

43. A USV will be arranged where you can see everything you need to from a public area such as a road and so have no need to go on to the appeal site. None of the parties to the appeal will attend.

Access required site visits (ARSV)

44. An ARSV will be arranged where you need to go onto the appeal site. It is important that you respond quickly when you are asked for site visit times.

Viewing the appeal site from a neighbouring property

45. The questionnaire asks the LPA “Will the Inspector need to enter a neighbour's land or property?” and has a space for the details if they say yes. Whilst the LPA may consider this essential, it is your decision whether to visit or not. If you do need to visit a neighbouring property, it will be undertaken as ARSV and the Case Officer will notify the neighbour of the date and time of your site visit.

## Conditions

46. If the LPA suggests any non-standard conditions you should consider whether the appellant should be given the opportunity to comment on them. However, some conditions would be unlikely to come as a surprise and so you would not need to seek comments - for example, obscure glazing a bathroom window or the ‘plans condition’. Consultation with the appellant will be required for pre-commencement conditions in the usual way. See the Conditions ITM chapter.

## Legal Agreements and Late Evidence

47. The Procedural Guide requires, for written reps appeals, the submission of a completed and executed agreement at the point the appeal is submitted. The appeal form asks the appellant if an agreement is to be submitted and asks for a copy to be downloaded.

<!-- Part1 p.280 -->

48. However, if a s106 is submitted after this time, you have the discretion, via Regulation 8(3) to disregard it. Indeed, caselaw (Akhtar, 2017) confirmed that even a material planning consideration can be disregarded where procedural regulations and guidance have not been complied with. These considerations will also apply where late evidence has been submitted. The default will be that it is not accepted and must be returned.

49. There may be exceptions which you need to consider. For example, Heads of Terms, ongoing negotiations about an Obligation, or other such information is evidenced to have been before the LPA during application stage but the Obligation was simply not signed and executed until after the appeal submission. If this is the case, and it is not clear from the paperwork, then you should clarify the situation with the Council, via your Case Officer, and you may accept the completed s106.

50. The parties may ask for a draft to be accepted, and whilst this is standard practise in oral events, it is your decision whether to accept it or not. In general, for written reps appeals, if an Obligation is submitted with an appeal in order to address a reason for refusal, (therefore it was not before the Council at any point in the application process) it should be turned away.

51. Regardless of whether you do or not, you must make it clear that you will not delay the determination of the appeal in order to wait for a fully executed one. You will need to carefully consider if the appeal can continue to be dealt with under Part 1, utilising Regulation 8(1) or whether it should be transferred to Part 2 so that appropriate consultation or publicity can be given to it.

52. If you have decided to disregard an executed Obligation, you will need to give reasons for this as a procedural matter. Remember that executed Section 106 agreements, whether unilateral or bilateral, may be binding on the parties whether or not you accept it as part of the appeal. You should consider carefully how to approach this situation if you are allowing the appeal, and there is an executed Obligation before you. See the Planning Obligations ITM chapter for further details.

## Costs applications

53. The 2008 Planning Act permits costs applications to be sought and awarded in written representations cases.

54. The appellant’s claim for costs should be made at the same time as the appeal. The LPA has 14 days from the start date of the appeal to make a claim. The party against whom the costs application has been made will be given an opportunity to comment within a set timescale. National guidance on the award of costs is provided in the Appeals section of the government’s ‘Planning Practice Guidance’.

<!-- Part1 p.281 -->

55. It is usual practice, where possible, to issue the appeal and costs decisions at the same time. However, it can be acceptable to issue the appeal decision first, to be followed by the Costs one. See the Costs Awards ITM chapter.

## Submitting the decision

56. Your completed decision should be sent to the case team for the Case Officer in the normal way. However, it is helpful to identify that it is a ‘Part 1 Decision’ in the subject bar of your e-mail. This helps the team identify and prioritise such cases.

57. The LPA will notify interested parties that they have a right to withdraw any application representations made within 4 weeks of the date the LPA letter is sent. Consequently, when sending your decision to despatch, it is helpful to note when this 4 week period will have passed (if it has not already) as the reasoning in a decision should not rely on a representation that has been withdrawn.

<!-- Part1 p.282 -->

The Inspector is seeking further information under Regulation 8 of The Town and Country Planning (Appeals) (Written Representations Procedure) (England) Regulations 2009.

[Insert details of the specific further information required]

The information must be provided in writing within 5 working days. [Longer if, exceptionally, the Inspector considers this necessary]

You are reminded that this is not an opportunity to provide any further information that has not been requested within this letter. Any such information will be disregarded and returned, unseen by the Inspector.

## Introduction

1. PINS Customer Quality Team (CQ) uses a wide definition of the term ‘complaint’. Any adverse comment about any aspect of an appeal decision is regarded as a complaint, regardless of whether the letter in general is couched in positive terms.

2. For example, a request for clarification, indicating that doubt exists over what is meant, is an implied complaint; and if it is found that the request has been necessitated by an error or wording that is genuinely capable of being misunderstood or confused, the complaint will be regarded as justified.

3. The greatest proportion (about 60%) of complaints comes from interested party objectors.

4. A complaint is an allegation that the Planning Inspectorate, in processing and deciding the casework for which it is responsible, did something material it shouldn't have done, or didn't do something material it should have done. In practice, this means that where there is still time to correct an error, and this is done, it will not be counted as a complaint, provided that it cannot have a material impact on the correct processing, or outcome, of the case. The definition of a Justified Complaint is therefore one where, following thorough and impartial investigation, the complaint is upheld.

5. JCs are categorised as either:

- Minor - judged not to have affected the outcome of the case, usually of little consequence. For example, errors of a typographical or minor factual nature, misspelled names etc are not included in the definition of justified complaint, as such errors would potentially be correctable under the Slip Rule. These are still recorded as errors so that Seconded Inspector Trainers (SITs) or Inspector Managers (IMs) can be made aware of any issues requiring remedial coaching or training.

- Significant – potentially affecting the outcome of the case or perceived by the public as prejudicial to a party’s interests. For example, if an Inspector fails to notice a window on an elevation of a dwelling opposite a proposed neighbouring extension where the issue is one of overlooking, the error

<!-- Part1 p.286 -->

may well be significant. If the window is located on another elevation where overlooking would not result, the error is more likely to be minor.

### Categories of justified complaints

- Improper conduct of site visit/hearing/inquiry.

- Taking into account an irrelevant factor / Failing to take into account/give appropriate weight to a relevant factor/ Misinterpreted a relevant factor or policy.

- Inadequate reasoning.

- Significant errors of judgement/perversity.

- Inclusion of unnecessary or inappropriate comments.

- Conditions errors/omissions/oversights.

- Failure to comply with rules of natural justice.

- In all instances where a clear error has occurred and this is agreed by the Inspector, CQ will reply without further input. Where there is any element of doubt or the issues are not clear-cut, CQ will seek not only the Inspector’s comments but also those of the Professional Lead (PL) (also the SIT for those in training) before coming to an independent view. The complaint would only be confirmed as justified with the agreement of the PL, or the Head of Planning Inspector Profession, should a disagreement arise.

- Once investigations are complete, CQ will reply, copying to Inspector’s IM and PL, with an appropriate explanation or apology, or both.

- The table below presents some tips for avoiding common causes of justified complaints.

### Potential | Check the following: problems

Factual matters Allowed/dismissed – are they the same in both decision and conclusion? Beware missing “not”s!

References, names, addresses, dates

LPA and parties’ names

Policy reference

<!-- Part1 p.287 -->

Compass points

Ascribe weight to emerging plans as appropriate, if they change anything

Show that you have had regard for any statutory requirements (but not necessary to state sections of Acts, etc)

SPG/SPD –Address compliance with the Regulations if contested and clarify the weight afforded if it adds anything

, where test is stronger (but avoid too much unnecessary description).

It is not sufficient simply to reach a view on any matter

– you must say why.

Deal with any relevant previous appeal decisions: if reaching a contrary conclusion, say why.

Where important, differentiate between matters of fact & those of personal judgement/opinion.

Do not engage in theorising or making unsubstantiated assumptions.

Don’t neglect interested parties’ views, particularly if relevant or well-researched: As mentioned above, about 60% of complaints are from them.

Do not be afraid of making third party views a main

<!-- Part1 p.288 -->

issue (if appropriate) simply because LPA have not refused on those grounds.

Don’t forget implementation clauses.

<!-- Part1 p.289 -->

Don’t rely on the computer spell-checker.

Avoid using double negatives – too easy to omit an important “not”.

Phrase main issues neutrally.

Use plain English

Write positively and concisely.

Be diplomatic.

Avoid making helpful comments

## The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman

6. The Ombudsman’s function is to investigate complaints by those who claim to have sustained injustice as a consequence of maladministration arising from action taken by or on behalf of a government department. The term maladministration encompasses such things as bias, neglect, incompetence, discourtesy, a failure to follow proper procedures and serious delay.

7. The Ombudsman’s powers are limited to the investigation of the administrative functions of government. S/he can therefore investigate to see whether there has been maladministration in the decision making process, but cannot change in any way an Inspector's decision.

8. The Ombudsman receives thousands of complaints a year, many of which are sifted out at an early stage. When the Ombudsman is satisfied that there is a case to answer they will write to the Chief Executive of PINS, setting out the details of the complaint and asking for a report. Inspectors involved in a complaint will be advised by PINS on the necessary procedures.

<!-- Part1 p.290 -->

## Annex A – Correction of Errors in Decisions (Slip Rule)

Part 5 of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004 (as amended) (the 2004 Act) allows the Inspectorate to issue a ‘Correction Notice’ to correct certain types of errors in decisions, provided that the error is contained in the decision document but does not form any part of the reasons given for the decision (see Section 59(5) of the 2004 Act). The provisions of the 2004 Act are only intended to correct obvious clerical mistakes, typographical errors, omissions or accidental slips, which are obvious to the parties concerned. By definition, correctable errors would not materially affect the reasoning in the decision if an amendment is made. The process for correcting such errors is often referred to as the “Slip Rule”.

Once issued, a corrected decision has full legal status, carries a fresh date (except for wrongly dated decisions – see below) and will replace (and be subject to the same provisions as) the original in all respects. The fresh date has the effect of resetting any High Court challenge period.

### What qualifies as a “Slip Rule” request?

The statutory requirements in Part 5 of the 2004 Act must be met before a correction notice is issued. A judgement has to be made as to whether the error in question is correctable under legislation and it is in the public interest to make the correction.

A “Slip Rule” request can be made by any person. In addition to the above criteria, for a request to be valid it must have been made in writing, relate to a decision type permitted to be corrected under legislation and submitted within the relevant High Court challenge period.

This criterion also applies to the Secretary of State or Inspectors who detect errors in their own decisions and wish to make a “Slip Rule” request.

### Registering and answering requests

The Customer Quality Team is responsible for recording and processing “Slip Rule” requests and making decisions on whether corrections should be made, having assessed the context of the request and sought comments from the appointed Inspector. The Customer Quality Team is also responsible for notifying the relevant parties about any intended correction.

Corrected decisions are sent to all parties who received a copy of the original decision. A procedural paragraph explains that the original decision has been superseded, with the following standard wording inserted above the first paragraph in the new decision, which reads:

“This decision is issued in accordance with Section 56(2) of the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004 (as amended) and supersedes the decision issued on …”

This paragraph is purposefully numberless, in order not to cause an effect on the existing paragraph numbers within the decision.

<!-- Part1 p.291 -->

The covering letter, referred to as the Correction Notice, specifies the correction of the error and accompanies the amended decision, which supersedes the original decision once issued.

In the circumstances where a correction is not made, the original decision continues to have full force and effect. That decision not to correct an error is communicated to the relevant parties by the Customer Quality Team, in accordance with Section 57(1)

(b) of the 2004 Act.

### Correcting Wrongly Dated Decisions

The “Slip Rule” should not be used where the error involves an incorrect date (or no date) on an issued decision. Such errors cannot be left uncorrected, however, as this could have major implications to the parties and the enforceability of a decision.

When such errors occur, the decision should be correctly dated and reissued by the relevant casework team to all parties who received the original decision, along with an apology and explanation for the mistake. It is legally necessary that the corrected decision date must be the date that the appeal decision was originally made – being the date that should have been correctly included in the decision in the first instance.

As it is not a “Slip Rule” change, responsibility for reissuing the appeal decision rests with the relevant casework team who issued the original decision. It is important for them to provide an explanation as to why the reissued decision is being sent. Any complaints arising from the reissuing of a decision will then be answered by the Customer Quality Team.

### Further information

For further information and assistance about the “Slip Rule” process, please contact the Customer Quality Team. “Slip Rule” requests received in any business area are forwarded to the Customer Quality Team as a priority matter. Colleagues in all business areas are responsible for:

Being aware that any person can make a “Slip Rule” request;

Identifying where such requests are made within correspondence sent to PINS; and

Notifying the Customer Quality Team (feedback@planninginspectorate.gov.uk) of requests that need to be considered in compliance with legislation.

The Customer Quality Team is responsible for handling all requests made, advising on the statutory requirements for “Slip Rule” and following the process for correcting decisions.
