269. The ‘transport impacts of the development, particularly to ensure safe site access’ is a prior approval matter for Class MA of Part 3 from 1 August 2021.

### Adequate Natural Light in all Habitable Rooms

270. The GPDO was amended by the Town and Country Planning (Permitted Development and Miscellaneous Amendments) (England) (Coronavirus) Regulations 2020 so that, for any prior approval application made on or after 1 August 2020, the matters for a change of use to a dwelling under Part 3, Classes M, N, O, PA and Q include the provision of ‘adequate natural light in all habitable rooms’.

271. NB –this prior approval matter has not been added to Part 3, paragraph P.2 since development is not permitted under Class P if the prior approval date falls on or after 10 June 2019; paragraph P.1(c).

<!-- Part2 p.27 -->

272. The prior approval matters for all classes of PD under Part 20 also include the provision of adequate natural light in all habitable rooms. Paragraph W.(2A) of Part 3 and paragraph B.(9) of Part 20 provide that prior approval must be refused in relevant applications if adequate natural light is not provided in all the habitable rooms of the dwellinghouse.

273. It should be noted, when assessing light levels, that obscure (or textured) glass has better light transmittance properties than clear glass, which has a more reflective outer surface, so less light passes through it. The Glass Handbook 2014 (Pilkington) states that obscure glass achieves transmittance of 0.86 for 6mm thick glass, whilst active clear glass (the clear glass with the highest light transmittance value) achieves only 0.83 (ie 3% less).

274. Where clear evidence is not available for assessing the amount of available light, it is important to seek the views of the parties before coming to a conclusion; Bounces Properties Ltd (Mr S Posen) v SSLUHC & Enfield LBC [2023] EWHC 735 (Admin).

275. The term ‘habitable rooms’ is defined in Part 3, paragraph X and Part 20, paragraph C.(1) as meaning ‘any rooms used or intended to be used for sleeping or living which are not solely used for cooking purposes, but does not include bath or toilet facilities, service rooms, corridors, laundry rooms, hallways or utility rooms’.

276. As noted above, from 6 April 2021, Article 3(9A) of the GPDO provides that Schedule 2 does not permit any new dwellinghouse where the gross internal floorspace is less than 37m2 or the dwellinghouse does not comply with the nationally described space standard issued by DCLG on 27 March 201522.

### Formal Decision

277. If a prior approval appeal is allowed – or there is a split decision – it is necessary to specify the nature of the development approved in relation to the correct Parts or Classes of the Order. For example, if dealing with a change of use to a dwelling under Part 3, Class Q, it would be necessary to specify if prior approval is granted for Q(a) only or Q(a) and Q(b).

278. It is essential that the decision refers not only to the relevant Part and Class, but also to Article 3(1) of the GPDO 2015, because it is that which grants planning permission for the development; see Annex G.

279. Consistent with decisions on s78 appeals, a decision allowing the appeal should refer to the date and reference of the application; it may be helpful in some instances to also incorporate plan reference numbers.

280. If the appeal is dismissed, irrespective of whether the LPA refused or failed to determine the application, the standard decision will suffice – although it will be necessary to specify the element of the development which is refused prior approval if there is a split decision.

[^22]: Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) (England) (Amendment) Regulations 2020/1243

<!-- Part2 p.28 -->

### Conditions

281. The Order imposes conditions on planning permissions granted under certain Parts and Classes. Such conditions should not be set out in the formal decision on a prior approval appeal, because the decision is not to grant planning permission but prior approval only. The decision will enable the conditions to bite by stating that ‘… prior approval is granted under the provisions of Article 3(1) and Schedule 2…’

282. To assist the parties, however, particularly the appellant, any relevant conditions imposed by the Order should be described in the Conclusion or Conditions section when allowing a prior approval appeal; see Annex G.

283. Decision-makers have sometimes imposed conditions on prior approval cases that are not imposed by the GPDO 2015. The GPDO itself does not provide any general authority for doing so, but there are specific powers available to LPAs and Inspectors. These will be given in the conditions section of the relevant class, so it is crucial that you check that particular class has the powers to impose such conditions.

284. So, it would be unnecessary and unreasonable to impose a matching materials condition in a Part 1, Class A case, because paragraph A.3 requires that the materials used in any exterior work other than in the construction of a conservatory shall be of a similar appearance to those used in the construction of the exterior of the existing dwelling.

285. It might be necessary and reasonable to restrict hours of operation, but only if required to address noise or traffic impacts where such matters are included in the prior approval requirements.

286. It would never be appropriate to require that development is commenced within a specified period, as per the s91 condition imposed on express permissions. A permission granted by the Order is continuous while the Order is in force or re-enacted, and unless the permission is revoked or withdrawn. Some PD is subject to a condition as to when the development must begin, and that should be set out in the conclusion to the decision.

287. The GPDO 2015 generally provides that, in respect of relevant Parts and Classes, development must be carried out in accordance with the approved details, or with the submitted details submitted where prior approval is not required. A ‘plans’ condition should only be imposed where necessary to ensure certainty, perhaps if minor amendments were a consideration.

288. As in any other appeal, it is not possible to impose a positively worded condition which requires the making of a planning obligation. Given the tests set out in PPG chapter 21a on ‘Use of Conditions’, a negatively worded condition may be imposed which prevent development from taking place until a specified matter has occurred. The Appeals against Conditions ITM advises on appeals against non-standard conditions imposed on prior approvals.

289. It was held in R (oao LW Zenith Ltd) v SSLUHC & Hart DC [2022] EWHC 3317 (Admin) that an Inspector erred in refusing to grant prior approval for a change of use under Class O on the basis that the proposed flats would lack adequate natural light as required under condition O.2(1)(e). There was an extant PP for operational development to install additional windows in the

<!-- Part2 p.29 -->

building, so imposing a negatively worded condition to prevent occupation of the proposed flats until the approved works had been carried out ‘was an obvious solution to allowing the change of use…by failing to have regard to this, the Inspector failed to have regard to a material consideration’.

290. As noted above, appeals may be made under s73 or s73A of the TCPA90 in respect of conditions imposed on a prior approval.

### Planning Obligations

291. PPG chapter 23b on ‘Planning Obligations’ advises in paragraph ref ID: 23b- 009-20190315 that, since PD should by nature be generally acceptable in planning terms, planning obligations would ordinarily not be necessary. Any entered into should concern matters requiring prior approval and not, for instance, affordable housing.

292. Regulation 122(1) of the Community Infrastructure Levy Regulations 2010 applies where a determination is made which results in a grant of planning permission. It does not apply to prior approval determinations where permission is granted under the Order and not by the LPA or Inspector.

293. Regulation 122(2), which specifies that a planning obligation may only constitute a reason for permitting the development if it is necessary, directly related and fairly and reasonably related in scale and kind, does not apply to prior approval determinations.

294. A planning obligation may be proffered, and should be considered in the planning balance, in mitigation of the matters that are the subject of the prior approval. Such an obligation would not be caught by the Regulation 123(3) pooling restriction. This is again because that provision only applies to the grant of planning permission.

295. Where applications are made for express planning permission, positively worded conditions to require an applicant to enter into a planning obligation should not be imposed. Negatively worded conditions may be imposed to that end ‘in exceptional circumstances’ and in relation to complex and strategically important development.

296. In prior approval appeals, it would not be necessary or reasonable to secure the provision of an obligation even by way of a negatively worded condition. It is only necessary to consider whether any obligation provides the necessary mitigation to prevent the refusal of prior approval.

### Other Statutory Duties

### European Sites

297. Regulation 9(1) of the Conservation of Habitats and Species Regulations 2017 requires an appropriate authority – including Inspectors – to exercise their functions (which are relevant to nature conservation) so as to secure compliance with the requirements of the Habitats and Wild Bird Directives. For the purposes of prior approval or other appeals concerned with the GPDO, however, Inspectors only need to be aware that Article 3(1) of the GPDO 2015 grants planning permission for the classes of development set out in Schedule 2 subject to Regulations 75-78.

<!-- Part2 p.30 -->

298. Regulation 75 provides that it is a condition of any PP granted by a general development order on or after 30 November 2017 that development which is

(a) likely to have a significant effect on a European site, alone or in combination with other plans or projects and (b) not directly connected with or necessary to the management of the site must not be begun until the developer has received the LPA’s written notification of approval of an application made under Regulation 7723.

299. Regulation 8(1) defines ‘European sites’ as Special Areas of Conservation (SACs) and candidate Special Areas of Conservation (cSACs) designated pursuant to the Habitats Directive; and Special Protection Areas (SPAs), designated pursuant to the Wild Birds Directive. Regulation 8(1) does not encompass, and therefore Regulations 75-78 do not apply to potential Special Protection Areas (pSPAs), sites identified or required as compensatory measures for adverse effects on European sites, proposed SACs (pSACs) and proposed or listed Ramsar sites24.

300. An application made to the LPA under Regulation 77 must include details of the development intended to be carried out, and a copy of any relevant notification by the appropriate nature conservation body – here being Natural England – under Regulation 76. The LPA must send a copy of the application to Natural England and take account of any representations they make.

301. Unless Natural England finds that the development is not likely to have a relevant effect, the LPA must make an appropriate assessment of the implications of the development for the European site in view of that site’s conservation objectives. The LPA may approve the Regulation 77 application only having ascertained that the development will not adversely affect the integrity of the European site.

302. Under Regulation 78(3)(a), a Regulation 75 (via Regulation 77) approval is to be treated as an approval required by a condition imposed on a grant of PP for the purposes of the appeals provisions of the TCPA90. In other words, Article 3(1) and Regulations 75-78 operate to impose a pre-commencement condition on all development that is permitted by the GPDO and would affect a European site. PD cannot be lawfully begun until the developer has made a Regulation 77 application and received written notification from the LPA to the effect that the development would have no adverse effect on the integrity of the European site.

303. As noted above, any requirement to seek prior approval before beginning PD is also a requirement to seek an approval required by a condition imposed on a grant of PP. However, neither the GPDO nor Regulations 75-78 prescribes the sequencing of prior approval and Regulation 77 applications. Developers do not need to obtain written notification of a Regulation 77 approval before

[^23]: Regulation 75 also applies to European offshore marine sites, within the meaning of Regulation 18 of the Offshore Marine Conservation Regulations.

[^24]: PSPAs and pSACs, and sites identified or required as compensatory measures for adverse effects on European sites, and proposed or listed Ramsar sites, are however given the same policy protection as European sites, under Framework paragraphs 187-191, for the purposes of any appeal made for express planning permission.

<!-- Part2 p.31 -->

seeking prior approval or vice versa25. It is only the case that the development cannot be lawfully begun until both procedures are complied with.

304. Thus, the Regulation 77 application may be submitted and approved after prior approval is given for the development. A prior approval appeal cannot be dismissed on the ground that a Regulation 77 application is required but not yet made or approved. If the LPA objects to an appeal on that basis, the Inspector should point out that, while the development cannot be begun until written notification is received of the approval of the Regulation 77 application, that does not need to precede the prior approval process.

305. A Regulation 77 application may be made before or at the same as one for prior approval. If a Regulation 77 application is approved by the time of writing a prior approval appeal decision letter, the Inspector may wish to note in a preliminary paragraph that Article 3(1) and the Regulations have been complied with (but it does not necessarily follow that the appeal will succeed). The Inspector can accept the LPA’s evidence as to whether they have received and approved any Regulation 77 application in respect of the European site; it is not necessary to go behind that conclusion.

306. There is a right of appeal against any LPA decision to refuse a Regulation 77 application. Any such appeal should be treated as being made under s78(1)(b) of the TCPA90 against a refusal of an approval required by a condition imposed on a grant of PP under Regulation 78(3)(a). It is possible that linked PA and Regulation 77 appeals will be before an Inspector.

307. There is no power to impose conditions on a Regulation 77 approval. Any necessary mitigation measures must be secured by way of a planning obligation or other legal agreement which will again be for the LPA to determine and outside of the prior approval process. Conditions imposed on grants of prior approval must be reasonably related to the PA matters.

### UK Protected Habitats and Species

308. S40 of the Natural Environment and Rural Communities Act 2006 requires that ‘every public authority must, in exercising its functions, have regard, so far as is consistent with the proper exercise of those functions, to the purpose of conserving biodiversity’. However, the GPDO does not – in Article 3(1) or otherwise – provide that PD is subject to the s40 duty.

309. While there is no legal authority to this effect, it is unlikely that any prior approval appeal, even where the matters include siting, location or amenity, could be seen as relating to the conservation of biodiversity for the purposes of s40 or planning policy; see the Natural Environment ITM chapter’s section on Permitted Development Rights for further information.

### Listed Buildings

310. S66 of the Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990 provides that: ‘…in considering whether to grant planning permission for development which affects a listed building or its setting, the local planning

[^25]: PPG paragraph 13-019-20190722 refers to the Article 3(1) and Regulations 73-76 limitations on PD, but it does not specify any sequence for Regulation 77 and prior approval applications.

<!-- Part2 p.32 -->

authority…shall have special regard to the desirability of preserving the building or its setting or any features of special architectural or historic interest which it possesses’.

311. The s66(1) duty does not generally apply to GPDO casework and is not directly relevant for prior approval applications because planning permission is granted by Article 3(1) of the GPDO. Some developments which would otherwise be PD are not so, however, if the building is listed.

312. Where the prior approval matters include amenity, siting or location, or design and external appearance, the impact of a development on the setting of a listed building will need to be assessed having regard to the policies on designated heritage assets in Chapter 20 of the Framework, particularly Policies HE4, HE5 and HE6.

### Conservation Areas

313. S72 of the Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990 provides that: ‘in the exercise, with respect to any buildings or other land in a conservation area, of any [functions under the Planning Acts]…special attention shall be paid to the desirability of preserving or enhancing the character or appearance of that area’.

314. The impact of development on a conservation area must be considered in prior approval cases where the matters are amenity, siting or location, or design and external appearance. As noted above, demolition of part of a gate or a wall in a conservation area will not be PD.

### Human Rights and the Public Sector Equality Duty

315. S3(1) of the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA98) states that, so far as it is possible to do so, primary legislation and subordinate legislation must be read and given effect in a way which is compatible with the Convention rights. However, human rights do not come into any determinations as to whether or not something is PD, because that is a question of law and the decision-maker has no discretion.

316. In R (oao Nunn) v First Secretary of State [2005] EWCA Civ 101, an enforcement notice against a telecoms mast was quashed on appeal [on ground (c)] because the LPA had failed to determine the prior approval application within the statutory period, prior approval was thus deemed to be granted and so the Inspector did not consider the merits of (and objections to) the mast. Their decision was challenged by an interested party on the basis that she had been denied her rights to a fair hearing under Article 6.

317. Lord Justice Waller held that the LPA had "infringed" Ms Nunn's Article 6 rights by failing to determine the prior approval application on time, but those rights were not engaged in the Inspector's decision on the ground (c) appeal. The Inspector could not have applied s3(1) of the HRA98 so as to find that there is no deemed prior approval or no lawful PP, or therefore to consider the merits of the mast on ground (a).

318. S3(1) of the HRA98 does not provide the court with jurisdiction to write words into the TCPA90 which would allow an Inspector to take away rights to begin development that is permitted by the GDPO. The planning scheme set out

<!-- Part2 p.33 -->

under the TCPA90 and GPDO could be operated compatibly with the Convention rights. That a legislative measure can be operated so as to violate an individual's Convention Rights, as the LPA operated the GPDO here, does not mean that the legislation is repugnant to the Convention.

319. R (oao Coventry Gliding Club Ltd) v Harborough BC [2020] EWHC 3388 (Admin) concerned a remedy hearing held after the claimant had successfully challenged the lawfulness of the LPA's decision to grant prior approval for a change of use under Part 3, Class Q, only for the parties to discover later that the LPA's decision had been out of time and the developer had the right to proceed anyway under paragraph W(11). Applying Nunn, the High Court held that paragraph W(11) was not incompatible with the Convention and there was no legal basis for an injunction preventing implementation of the PD.

320. The SoS addressed the applicability of the HRA98 in respect of nearby occupiers in a prior approval appeal (APP/X5210/A/14/2212605) for a Part 3, Class J (now MA) change of use from offices to dwellinghouses. Local residents objected that the development would harm their living conditions and violate their Article 8 rights to private and family lives and homes.

321. Since the prior approval matters for Class J did not include "amenity", the SoS concluded that LPAs and Inspectors should proceed on the basis that the relevant Parts and Classes of the Order are compatible with Article 8. The grant of prior approval in any particular case will be justified under Article 8(2) by the general benefits of the legislation, even if there is a sufficiently serious impact to raise an issue under Article 8(1).

322. It follows that the human rights of interested parties or nearby occupiers are not engaged in prior approval appeals if and where the matters do not allow for consideration – using Article 8 as an example – of the impact of the development on those persons' private and family lives and homes. If the matters do not encompass such issues, Inspectors should assume that the relevant Part and Class is compliant with Article 8, with the grant of permission being proportionate and justified under Article 8(2).

323. If and where the prior approval matters do allow for consideration of issues which engage human rights, and the evidence is relevant, Inspectors should ensure their decision is compatible with the Convention rights. For example, where the matters include "amenity" and the representations include that the development would harm the neighbour's living conditions, Inspectors should evaluate the issues and weigh their findings in a balancing exercise which is informed (explicitly or by implication) by the neighbour's Article 8 rights. It should be shown that any decision to interfere with such rights, including the best interests of any children, is proportionate.

324. The public sector equality duty (PSED) set out under s149 of the Equality Act 2010 does not come into any determination as to whether or not something is PD. Where the matters allow for consideration of particular impacts of a grant of prior approval on interested parties or nearby occupiers with protected characteristics, the Inspector should evaluate those impacts and weigh them in the balance with due regard to the aims of the PSED. However, the duty to have due regard does not dictate the outcome, as held in the context of a prior approval appeal in R (oao Patel) v SSCLG & Johal & Wandsworth BC [2016] EWHC 3354 (Admin).

<!-- Part2 p.34 -->

325. The Courts have not tested the question as to whether the appellant's human rights and/or protected characteristics are engaged in prior approval cases where the development relates to the appellant's home – and is perhaps designed to meet particular family needs – but such needs for or benefits of the development fall outside of the prior approval matters. Any such submissions should be raised with Knowledge Centre.

326. Further information is provided in the Human Rights and Equality chapter.

<!-- Part2 p.35 -->

## Annex A: Part 1 – Development in the Curtilage of a Dwellinghouse

### Interpretation of Part 1

General

1. Part 1 appeals casework must be considered in the light of the definitions set out in Article 2(1); Schedule 2, Part 1, Paragraph I of the Order; and in the latest or relevant version of the Technical Guidance.

2. The Technical Guidance is only relevant to Part 1 and cannot be read across to provide guidance for any other Part. Even if the development is within the curtilage of a dwellinghouse, if the relevant Part is not Part 1 (for example, the question is whether a fence is PD under Part 2) then the Technical Guidance does not apply.

3. As noted above, the entire demolition of dwellinghouses constitutes development which requires planning permission. Such works would be PD if compliant with Article 3 and Schedule 2, Part 11, Class B. The rebuilding of a dwellinghouse also falls outside of the permission granted by Article 3 and Schedule 2, Part 126.

4. The PD rights granted under Part 1 do not apply to dwellings permitted under other Parts, with some inconsistencies:

- Limitations A.1(a), B.1(a), C.1(a), D.1(a), E.1(a), F.1(a), G.1(a) and H.1(a) provide that development is not permitted under Part 1, Classes A, B, C, D, E, F, G or H if permission to use the dwellinghouse as such was granted only by virtue of Part 3, Class G, M, MA, N, P, PA or Q.

- Limitation AA.1(a) provides that development is not permitted under Part 1, Class AA if permission to use the dwellinghouse as such was granted only by virtue of Class G, M, MA, N, O, P, PA or Q of Part 3.

- Limitations A.1(l), B.1(g), C.1(d), D.1(e), E.1(k), F.1(b), G.1(d), H.1(f) provide that development is not permitted under Part 1, Classes A, B, C, D, E, F, G or H if the dwellinghouse was built under Part 20. There is no equivalent limitation for development permitted under Part 1, Class AA.

- Limitation B.1(h) provides that development is not permitted under Part 1, Class B if the existing dwellinghouse has been enlarged in reliance on the permission granted by Class AA. In other words, where the Class AA PD rights have been exercised to construct an additional storey, Class B does not grant permission for any enlargement of the roof of that additional storey. There is no equivalent limitation on any other Class under Part 1.

5. Certain types of development are not permitted under Classes A, B, E, G or H in respect of dwellinghouses on Article 2(3) land. The same applies to Class AA, where development is also not permitted in SSSIs.

[^26]: Sainty v MHLG [1963] 15 P&CR 432; Larkin v SSE [1980] JPL 407; Hewlett v SSE [1983] JPL 155.

<!-- Part2 p.36 -->

### Permitted Development for Householders: Technical Guidance

6. As with the Order, prior approval appeals should be considered with regard to the current edition of the Technical Guidance. Since this was published in September 2019, it does not advise on PD under Class AA of Part 1.

7. In Enforcement and LDC appeals, it may be necessary to refer to the Technical Guidance in force on the relevant date. It is guidance, and not a statutory instrument like the Order itself.

8. The Library has retained copies of the original August 2010 version, and the updated versions from January 2013, October 2013, April 2014, April 2016 and April 2017. NB: the October 2013 version was itself modified twice. All versions are available via the Library.

9. Where parties cite an interpretation of the Technical Guidance in a past appeal decision, Inspectors should establish whether a different version of the Guidance then existed, and if the present appeal can be distinguished.

10. Where the Technical Guidance is material, this is as an aid to interpretation and application of the Order. The starting point should still be, so far as possible, the wording of the Order itself. That said, where the Guidance clearly covers the issue at hand, it should be followed unless it has been overturned by the Courts or does not apply to the particular facts of the case.

11. The Technical Guidance not only sets out definitions of terms as in the Order, but also guidance on terms which are not defined in the Order. Some terms are listed in the General Issues section at the start; others are defined in relation to particular Classes. The Guidance also includes diagrams to illustrate terminology and whether development would be PD.

12. The phrase ‘so far as practicable’ in Part 1, paragraphs A.3(c), B.2(b) and H.2(b) is not defined in the GPDO 2015 or Technical Guidance but, as set out below, the latter gives assistance in respect of B.2(b). The onus is on the applicant to show it would not be ‘practicable’ to comply with the conditions.

13. The Technical Guidance advises that, when considering whether a proposal is PD, all relevant Parts and Classes within those Parts need to be considered.

Eaves

14. There are two definitions for eaves in the Technical Guidance. In relation to Class A, the Guidance explains that for the purpose of measuring ‘height’ from ‘ground level’, ‘the eaves of a house are the point where the lowest point of a roof slope, or a flat roof, meets the outside wall.

15. Eaves height is measured in accordance with Article 2(2) from [the highest point of] the natural ground level at the base of the outside wall to the point where that wall would meet the upper surface of the roof slope. Parapet walls and any overhang should be ignored for the purposes of measurement, as set out on p11-12 of the Technical Guidance.

16. The Technical Guidance also states that, for the purposes of Class B and condition B.2(b), the measurement of an enlargement to the roof should be made along the original roof slope from the outermost edge of the eaves (or

<!-- Part2 p.37 -->

edge of the tiles or slates) to the edge of the enlargement. Any guttering that protrudes beyond the roof slope should not be included.

17. The latter interpretation of the Order in the Technical Guidance was successfully challenged in the High Court27 but the Order itself was then amended such that the Technical Guidance is correct. For enforcement and LDC appeals, the GPDO 2015 is stricter than the GPDO 1995 in relation to retention of eaves under B.2(b).

Obscure glazing

18. Conditions A.2(b)(i), B.2(c)(i) and C.2(a) require particular windows to be ‘obscure-glazed’. That phrase is not defined in the Order but is in the Technical Guidance: ‘Glazing to provide privacy is normally rated on a scale of 1-5, with 5 providing the most privacy. To be permitted development, side windows should be obscure glazed to minimum of level 3. Obscure glazing does not include one-way glass’.

19. The phrase ‘level 3’ does not refer to any British Standard; it is likely to be a manufacturer’s (such as Pilkington) categorisation. Whether development with a relevant window that is obscure glazed to less than level 3 is PD would be a question for the decision-maker.

### Implementing a Separate Planning Permission & Part 1 PD Rights

20. It was held in R (oao Watts) v SSETR [2002] JPL 1473 that, when assessing whether development is permitted by the Order, the question is whether, from the start of the development until its substantial completion, the building has been otherwise enlarged, improved or altered by more than the specified allowances. If it has, the development would cease to be permitted by the Order and can be enforced against.

21. Watts may be relevant where express PP is granted say for a ground floor extension to a dwelling, and the owners seek to use their Part 1 allowance first, perhaps by constructing a dormer extension. In an Enforcement or LDC case in particular, the Inspector may need to assess whether the end result comprises development in accordance with the PP and the PD right.

22. Sometimes it is claimed that changes from the permitted plans made to a dwelling during its erection have been made with the benefit of PD rights under Part 1. The general principle is that PD rights are not available until a dwellinghouse has been substantially completed, even if the changes would have been PD had they been carried out to the completed dwelling; R (oao Townsley) v SSCLG [2009] EWHC 3522.

23. The underlying logic is that the dwellinghouse does not exist as such until it has been substantially completed. It follows from the Gravesham test that a partly constructed building could not provide all the facilities necessary for day to day living. Moreover, once the construction of the dwellinghouse has departed in a material way from what permission was granted for, the building has become unlawful and PD rights do not apply by virtue of Article 3(5).

[^27]: Waltham Forest LBC v SSCLG (QBD) 18 June 2013

<!-- Part2 p.38 -->

24. The meaning of ‘substantial completion’ is as set out in Sage v SSETR [2003] UKHL 22: that the building operation would need to be carried out, both externally and internally, fully in accordance with the permission. A different definition applied in Watts has been superseded by Sage.

### Class A – General Considerations

Curtilage

25. The Technical Guidance defines curtilage as ‘land which forms part and parcel with the house. Usually, it is the area of land within which the house sits, or to which it is attached, such as the garden, but for some houses, especially…properties with large grounds, it may be a smaller area’.

26. Since PD rights only apply when the development fully accords with the limitations set out in the GPDO 2015, it is implicit that works subject to Part 1 are within the curtilage of a dwellinghouse. There cannot be any infringement of that requirement. Indeed, the concept of ‘de minimis’ does not apply to breach of any GPDO limitation or condition.

‘Enlarged Part of the Dwellinghouse’

27. It was held in Kensington and Chelsea RBC v SSCLG [2015] EWHC 2458 (Admin) that the ‘enlarged part of the dwellinghouse’ does not include the ‘original’ building but does include previous enlargements.

28. That judgment was contradicted in Hilton v SSCLG & Bexley LBC [2016] EWHC (Admin), where it was held that the term refers only to development comprising the enlargement of a dwellinghouse proposed to be carried out under Class A. Thus, the term ‘enlarged part of the dwellinghouse’ is now defined in the Technical Guidance as ‘the enlargement which is proposed to be carried out under Class A’.

29. The Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) (England) (Amendment) Order 2017/391 inserted limitation A.1(ja): development is not PD where ‘any total enlargement (being the enlarged part together with any existing enlargement of the original dwellinghouse to which it will be joined) exceeds or would exceed the limits set out in [A.1](e) to (j)’. A.1(ja) applies to PA appeals under A.1(g) except where information was provided to the LPA under A.4(2) before 6 April 2017.

30. Paragraph A.2 provides that development is not permitted under Class A if the dwellinghouse is on Article 2(3) land and it would consist or include ‘the cladding of any part of the exterior of the dwellinghouse with stone, artificial stone, pebble dash, render, timber, plastic or tiles’. The term ‘dwellinghouse’ is not qualified here and thus not restricted to the original dwellinghouse.

31. It follows, for Class A, that if a house on Article 2(3) land is already (eg) clad in render, and an extension is proposed to be rendered in order to comply with the matching materials condition under A.3(a), the extension would not be PD because it would conflict with A.2(a).

Demolition

<!-- Part2 p.39 -->

32. If operations proposed under Part 1 would involve partial demolition, it will be a matter of fact and degree as to whether the works would be excluded from development under s55(2)(g) and Article 3(9).

33. If it is proposed to build an extension under Part 1, Class A following the partial demolition of the dwellinghouse, the part to be demolished should be considered as a part of the original dwelling, even if the demolition works themselves would not require planning permission.

34. For example, if it is proposed to demolish an original outrigger and replace it with a wider rear extension, then the replacement extension should be assessed on the basis that it would ‘extend beyond a wall forming a side elevation of the original dwellinghouse’ for the purpose of A.1(j).

Principal, Rear and Side Elevations

35. The limitations set out in A.1(e) to A.1(j) refer to the ‘principal’, ‘rear’ and ‘side’ elevations of the original dwellinghouse; the Technical Guidance assists in interpretation of those terms. There may be more than one ‘rear wall’, for example, where the original rear wall is stepped. Measurement must be taken from the part of the wall being extended from.

36. Similarly, Inspectors are advised to measure the width or depth of the ‘enlarged part of the dwellinghouse’ for the purposes of A.1(e)-(j), and also for A.1(ja), A.2(b)-(d) and A.4(2), by measuring between the elevations of the enlargement – and discounting any roof overhang28.

37. Where the enlarged part would extend beyond a wall forming a side elevation of the original dwellinghouse, failure to meet any of the limitations in A.1(j)(i) to (iii) would take the development out of PD. The Technical Guidance indicates that a wall forming a side elevation will be any that cannot be identified as being a front wall or a rear wall. A.1(j) will apply where a passageway wall forms a side wall to the original dwellinghouse, notwithstanding that the wall is covered by a first floor.

38. If part of the original dwellinghouse has been demolished since the relevant date, the remainder of the building would count as part of the original. But any adjoining structure would not be considered as part of the dwellinghouse unless that is shown to be the case as a matter of fact and degree.

39. If the proposed extension would extend beyond the line of an original side elevation, but that wall was previously demolished or would be demolished as part of the proposed development, the restrictions in A.1.(j) would apply. The limitations to PD are based on the original dwellinghouse and apply if part of the original is removed.

40. Inspectors should note that rear extensions need to be assessed against the restrictions on side extensions where they also extend beyond a side wall. Whether there is a side wall or not is a question of fact and degree. Inspectors

[^28]: The roof of the enlargement would be considered when measuring height, for example, for the purposes of A.1(c) and (d). The roof would also be considered where there are limitations pertaining to “any part of the structure”; for example, in Part 1, Class D, paragraph D.1(d).

<!-- Part2 p.40 -->

should be aware that even a very short and/or shallow wall could constitute a ‘side wall’ for the purposes of the Order.

41. The only possible exception would be if an Inspector found, as a matter of fact and degree, that the protrusion was too shallow to constitute a wall. A window sill, for example, would not normally constitute a side wall, but a projection in the brickwork might be identifiable as such.

Opposite Boundary

42. Kensington established that the test in A.1(h)(ii) means that there must be 7m from the rear wall of the application dwelling to the opposite boundary. This judgment was not contradicted by Hilton.

43. Paragraph A.1(h)(ii) was amended in April 2016 to preclude development with more than a single storey within 7m of any boundary of the curtilage of the dwelling being enlarged opposite the rear wall of that dwelling29. The Technical Guidance states that an enlargement with more than one storey ‘must be a minimum of 7m away from any boundary of its curtilage which is opposite the rear wall of the house being enlarged.’ Therefore, an extension will be within 7m of the boundary if it is a minimum of 7m away. The Technical Guidance also suggests on page 20, albeit in relation to the depth of an extension, that measurement should be from the base of the wall.

Subterranean or Basement Extensions

44. The planning permission granted by Part 1, Class A, for enlargements, improvements or alterations to a dwellinghouse could potentially allow for a basement extension subject to the limitations set out in A.1(e) to (ja).

45. It was held in Eatherley v Camden LBC [2016] EWHC 3108 (Admin) that it may be necessary to assess whether engineering works required for a basement extension would be PD under Class A. There had to be a point where the excavation, underpinning and support for a basement differed in character from the enlargement, improvement and alteration of the dwelling. It is for the decision-maker to decide whether there were one or two activities of substance as a matter of fact and degree.

### Class A – Prior Approval Matters

No Consultation by LPA

46. If the LPA did not carry out the necessary consultation, they must be asked to do so (via the Case Officer) if and before the Inspector seeks to allow appeal. Prior approval cannot be granted if the owners or occupiers of any premises or land adjoining the site were not properly consulted.

Objections and Impact on Amenity

47. For Part 1, Class A, paragraph A.4(7) is triggered where an objection is before the decision-maker, or the developer is required to submit further information. An Inspector cannot raise their own concerns or have regard to the question

[^29]: Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) (England) (Amendment) Order 2016/332

<!-- Part2 p.41 -->

of amenity unless there had been a representation from a neighbour which triggers the need for the prior approval.

48. If the LPA notified neighbouring properties, no objections were received, and the development could be PD, the appeal should be allowed on the basis that prior approval is not required, and it is not possible to impose conditions.

49. If the need for prior approval is triggered by a relevant representation, the development should be assessed on the basis of its impact on the amenity of all ‘adjoining’ premises and land, including those where the occupiers did and did not make representations.

Fallback Position

50. While A.4(7) is only triggered when there is an objection or the developer is required to submit further information, it is still worth bearing in mind that – when addressing any fallback position – the outcome of the prior approval procedure cannot be guaranteed in the same way as PD without a pre-commencement condition. Neighbours may change, and so may the opinions of neighbours.

51. Where a proposal might result in injury to amenity, the LPA must have regard to whether the development would be compatible with Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights as incorporated into domestic law in the Human Rights Act 1998. The GPDO must be read under s3 of the Human Rights Act in ‘a way which is compatible with the Convention rights’, making it necessary to have regard to impacts on residential amenity where that is within the prior approval matters.

Objective Test

52. Overall, the assessment of impact on amenity must be objective, ie, consider the amenities that should reasonably be enjoyed by occupiers of neighbouring properties generally, rather than subjective preferences.

53. Objections often made in such cases include a claim to a ‘right to a view’ or of a loss in value of adjoining property. It is useful to bear in mind the observations of Ouseley J in R (oao) Cummins & others v Camden LBC & SSETR [2001] EWHC Admin 1116:

‘The private view from a window is not of itself regarded as a planning matter. There may well be a public interest in the protection of the character of an area which may be affected by a development and the impact on a view from a window may also be reflected in a wider loss of residential amenity; indeed in certain circumstances the change of view for an individual may have an impact to such an extent on the residential amenities enjoyed by the property that it does constitute a planning consideration.

‘But normally a change of view from for example, a view over green fields to a view over a new housing estate, is not regarded as a planning consideration even though it may have a financial impact on the value of the houses which lose the view over hitherto open land. The operation of the planning system would have to change if such an impact is regarded as determining a civil right by reference to the value of the property, and yet cannot of itself be considered relevant.’

<!-- Part2 p.42 -->

### Class AA

54. The GPDO was amended on 31 August 2020 to introduce Class AA to Part 1 of Schedule 2, setting out PD rights for development consisting of works for the construction of up to two additional storeys on an existing dwellinghouse that consists of two or more storeys, or one additional storey on an existing single storey dwellinghouse, together with any reasonably necessary engineering operations.

55. Development is permitted under Class AA subject to limitations and conditions including a requirement to apply for prior approval. The development must not begin until written notice is received of the grant of prior approval.

56. Paragraph AA.1(c) provides that development is not permitted under Class AA if ‘the dwellinghouse was constructed before 1 July 1948 or after 28 October 2018’. Given the word ‘constructed’, AA.1(c) should be interpreted as referring to the date of the erection of the building rather than the date of the commencement of the use, if that occurred later.

57. Paragraph AA.1(i) states that development is not permitted by Class AA if the additional storeys are constructed other than on the ‘principal part’ of the building. Paragraph AA.4(1) defines ‘principal part’ as meaning ‘the main part of the dwellinghouse excluding any front, side or rear extension of a lower height, whether this forms part of the original dwellinghouse or is a subsequent addition’.

58. The Technical Guidance 2019 advises on establishing the principal part of a building. Although this refers to its usage in Class A cases, there is no reason that this should not also apply to Class AA. However, the term ‘extension’ is not itself defined in the GDPO and so whether any of the building is an extension or not will be a matter of planning judgment for the decision maker.

59. It should not be assumed that lower parts of the building are automatically ‘extensions’ where additional storeys cannot be constructed under AA.1(i). Components of the building which are the same height as or higher than the main part should also be assessed on a fact and degree basis, but the terms ‘main part’ and ‘extension’ should be treated as mutually exclusive. The part of the building in question may be one or the other but not both.

60. Development is in any event not permitted under Class AA if permission to use the dwellinghouse as such was granted by virtue of Part 3 of the Order – or if the building contains more than a single dwellinghouse. None of the PD classes set out under Part 1 apply to flats or buildings containing flats because of how the term ‘dwellinghouse’ is defined in Article 2(1).

### Classes B and C

61. Class B permits “the enlargement of a dwellinghouse consisting of an addition or alteration to its roof.” Class C permits “any other alteration to the roof of a dwellinghouse”, so works may fall under either class. Parapet walls, railings, trellises and other barriers will generally be regarded as additions or alterations to the roof, to be considered under Class B, rather than Class A; see Richmond-upon-Thames LBC v SSE & Neale [1991] JPL 948. Class B does not apply at all to Article 1(5) land; only Class C grants any PD rights to the roofs of dwellings in such areas

<!-- Part2 p.43 -->

62. Class C permits works such as re-roofing in a different style, material or colour where that would constitute ‘development’ by virtue of a material effect on the external appearance of the building; s55(2)(a)(ii).

63. Class C PD rights apply to the installation of roof lights or other alterations that would protrude by no more than more than 150mm beyond the plane of the slope of the original roof and be no higher than the highest part of the original roof. If roof lights would as a matter of fact and degree alter the shape of roof or materially enlarge the dwelling viewed as a whole, the development should be considered under Class B.

### Class B

64. Works do not need to have a volume to be regarded as an "enlargement" for the purposes of Class B. In Richmond, the Court held that, even though they provided no more usable space for the dwelling, the parapet walls appeared to the objective observer as an enlargement of the dwelling house and so within Class B, provided they met all the limitations of that Class.

65. In such cases, it is not right to regard the whole empty space enclosed by (for example) parapet walls as increasing the cubic content for the purposes of provisos B.1(c) and (d). But the Richmond case also indicates that, for the purposes of proviso B.1(a), the height of the highest part of the existing roof refers to the roof as a whole and not just the flat roof of the extension.

66. It was confirmed in R (oao Cousins) v Camden LBC [2002] EWHC 324 (Admin) that the correct test is set out in Richmond: does the house appear larger to those outside looking at it? The railings did not enlarge the external appearance of the dwelling and so fell within Class C, but the position might have been different had a parapet wall been constructed as in Richmond. The question of whether parapet walls, railings, trellises and other barriers fall within Class B or C will need to be assessed as a matter of fact and degree.

67. It is sometimes argued that walls, railings and trellises are means of enclosure and permitted under Class A of Part 2. DCLG (as then) advice, which has not been challenged in the High Court, is that the top of a parapet wall or other enclosure on a flat roof of a single storey extension must by definition be more than 2m above ground level and therefore cannot be PD under that heading.

68. Development is not PD under paragraph B.1(d) if the cubic content of the resulting [from the enlargement to the] roof space would exceed the cubic content of the original roof space by more than (i) 40m3 in the case of a terrace house, or (ii) 50m3 in any other case. There is no definition of ‘roof space’ – but ‘cubic content’ is defined in Article 2(1) as ‘the cubic content of a structure or building measured externally’.

69. It was held in Havering LBC v SSCLG [2017] EWHC (Admin) 1546 that, when applying B.1(d), “what…is clearly intended is that one looks at the roof rather than any question of roof space, and space is simply added not to require going into the what might have been originally under the roof, but the roof itself and any addition or extension to that roof as it originally stood”. The dormer was to be measured externally and it would breach B.1(2)(d).

70. Paragraph B.2(b) provides that the enlargement must be constructed so that:

<!-- Part2 p.44 -->

(i) Other than in the case of a hip-to-gable enlargement or an enlargement which joins the original roof to the roof of a rear or side extension (aa) the eaves of the original room are maintained or reinstated; and (bb) the edge of the enlargement closest to the eaves of the original roof is, so far as practicable, not less than 0.2 metres from the eaves, measured along the roof slope from the outside edge of the eaves; and

(ii) Other than in the case of an enlargement which joins the original roof to the roof of a rear or side extension, no part of the enlargement extends beyond the outside face of any external wall of the original dwellinghouse30.

71. The Technical Guidance advises on the meaning of “so far as practicable” for B.2(b)(i)(bb):

“This 0.2m set back will be required unless it can be demonstrated that this is not possible due to practical or structural considerations…[for example] where a dormer on a side extension of a house joins an existing or proposed dormer on the main roof of the house”.

72. The Technical Guidance can also be interpreted to suggest that an ‘L-shaped dormer’ which connects the main roof of a dwellinghouse to that of an outrigger or extension would normally be “an enlargement… which joins the original roof to the roof of a rear or side extension”, meaning that it is exempt from conditions B.2(b)(i)(aa) and (bb) and B.2(b)(ii).

73. In Enforcement and LDC appeals concerning B.2(b), it will be necessary for the Inspector to consider how the enlargement is constructed on a fact and degree basis, and explain their conclusion accurately, including why that might differ from other appeal decisions which appear to concern the same type of enlargement.

### Class E

74. In enforcement and LDC appeals concerning Class E, it may be necessary to consider whether the development is or would be within the curtilage of the dwellinghouse as described above.

75. Another dispute which arises in such appeals is whether the proposed building is required for ‘a purpose incidental to the enjoyment of the dwellinghouse as such’.

76. The meaning of ‘incidental’ uses is considered in the Enforcement chapter. In short, however, an incidental use must have a functional relationship with the primary use, and the relationship should be one that is normally found. It is not founded on the personal choice of the person carrying out both activities together; Harrods v SSETR [2002] JPL 1258.

77. Where a building within the curtilage of a dwellinghouse would contain primary living accommodation, such as bedrooms or a kitchen, it would be in residential use, not in use for purposes incidental to a residential use. It would not normally be PD under Class E. (It would probably be used as part and

[^30]: Paragraph B.4 exempts roof tiles, guttering, fascias, barge boards and other minor roof details overhanging the external wall of the original dwellinghouse from B.2(b)(ii).

<!-- Part2 p.45 -->

parcel of the existing dwellinghouse or be used as a separate dwellinghouse following a material change of use to subdivide the planning unit.)

78. In Peche D’or Investments v SSE [1996] JPL 311 it was acknowledged that while a study would normally be regarded as an integral part of use as a dwellinghouse, a fact and degree assessment should be made as to whether that is so in each case. There was no warrant in the legislation for exclusion of a particular type of room or building from Class E rights as a matter of law.

79. It was subsequently held in Rambridge v SSE & East Herts DC (QBD 22.11.96 CO-593-96) that, in order to comprise PD, all of the building proposed under Class E must be required for purposes incidental to the dwellinghouse. A building that is in a mixed use or used for a primary residential purpose, such as a bedroom, cannot be PD under Class E.

80. The Court in Emin v SSE [1989] JPL 909 confirmed that regard should be had not only to the use to which the Class E building would be put, but also to the nature and scale of that use in the context of whether it was a purpose incidental to the enjoyment of the dwellinghouse.

81. The physical size of the building in comparison to the dwellinghouse might be part of that assessment but is not by itself conclusive. It is necessary to identify the purpose and incidental quality in relation to the enjoyment of the dwelling and answer the question as to whether the proposed building is genuinely and reasonably required or necessary in order to accommodate the proposed use or activity and thus achieve that purpose.

82. Paragraph E.1(c) provides that buildings are not PD if they are on ‘land forward of a wall forming the principal elevation of the original dwellinghouse’. This limitation covers all of the area in front of the ‘principal elevation’ as defined in the Technical Guidance, being usually but not always the elevation which fronts the ‘main highway serving the house’.

83. Paragraph E.1(e) applies a height limitation to a ‘dual pitched roof’; the Technical Guidance specifically states that this limitation should be applied to hipped roofs, but it does not mention any other roof type. Inspectors should take the term as encompassing gabled as well as hipped roofs but not mansard or gambrel roofs, or roofs with two pitches on each side.

84. The restriction under E.1(e)(ii) on the height of the building within 2m of the boundary applies to the whole building. It is not possible to sub-divide the building into parts of differing heights. E.1(e) applies if the development would comprise works for the ‘maintenance, improvement or other alteration’ of an existing building which already exceeds the height limitations – and even if the proposed works would not make serve to make the building any higher.

85. However, height should still be measured in accordance with Article 2(2) and the Technical Guidance; from the highest ground level immediately adjacent to the building. Distance to the boundary should be measured as advised above in relation to Class A: from the base of the building and on the basis that "within 2m" means that 2m is the minimum permitted distance.

86. It was held in McGaw v the Welsh Ministers & the Council for the City and County of Swansea [2020] EWHC 2588 (Admin) that where an LDC was sought for proposed development under Class E and the appellant proposed

<!-- Part2 p.46 -->

to backfill the land, the Inspector was wrong to base his assessment of height on existing ground levels. The judgment was not appealed on that point.

87. The case was considered by the CoA with respect to what ground should be considered ‘adjacent’ to the southern flank of the building when it would abut the curtilage boundary. The boundary wall could not be taken as the adjacent ground. It was held in McGaw v Welsh Ministers [2021] EWCA Civ 976 that the adjacent ground did not have to be within the curtilage of the appeal dwellinghouse. On the facts, it was right to identify the neighbour’s garden as the immediately adjacent ground for the purposes of Class E.

88. The approach set out in these judgments should be followed but Inspectors should also note that:

- Class E does not expressly permit engineering operations and so it may be necessary to assess whether any proposed works to alter land levels would in fact be PD as per Eatherley described above.

- Class E and indeed Part 1 is concerned with development in the curtilage of a dwellinghouse. Neither the Order nor Technical Guidance indicates that land outside of the curtilage may be the reference point for measuring height. Any decision to measure height from the neighbouring property should be fully justified on the facts of the case.

<!-- Part2 p.47 -->

## Annex B: Part 3 – Changes of Use

1. Part 3 of the GPDO 2015 sets out Classes of [material] changes of use and, in some cases, associated operational development which are granted PP. Part 3 has been amended through various Orders since 2015, with the result being the revocation of some Classes and changes to others. The revoked Classes are B, C, D, E, J, JA, K, O and PA. Queries relating to amendments and transitional arrangements should be sent to Knowledge Centre.

2. Some PD rights set out under other Parts and Classes are disapplied to uses permitted under Part 3. For example, the PP granted under Part 1, Class A to enlarge a dwellinghouse does not apply, under A.1(a), if permission to use the dwellinghouse as such was granted by Part 3, Class G, M, MA, N, P, PA or Q.

### Prior Approval Requirements

3. All of the permitted changes in Part 3 are subject to limitations and conditions, but only some are subject to a pre-commencement condition requiring a prior approval procedure.

- Development is permitted under Part 3, Classes G, M, MA, N, P, Q, S and T subject to conditions G.1(d), M.2(1), MA.2(1), N.2(1), P.2(b), Q2.(1), S.2(1)(b) and T.2(1)(b) that, before beginning the development, the developer must apply to the LPA for a determination as to whether their prior approval will be required in relation to specified matters.

- The same applies to development permitted under Part 3, Class R above a floorspace threshold discussed below; R.3(1)(b). Below that, it is only necessary for the developer to provide information to the LPA; R.3(1)(a).

- The PD rights set out under Classes O, P and PA expired on 31 July 2021,10 June 2019 and 1 October 2020, via O.2(2)(b), P.1(c) and PA.1(c) respectively, but were subject to a prior approval procedure.

- Development is permitted under Part 3, Class A subject to condition A.1 that, before beginning the development, the developer provides written notification to the LPA of the date on which the use will change. No other class under Part 3 is subject to a notification or prior approval condition.

4. Part 3, paragraph W sets out the procedure for applications for prior approval under Part 3. Paragraph W.10(b) requires the decision-maker to ‘have regard to the National Planning Policy Framework…so far as relevant to the subject matter of the prior approval, as if the application were a planning application’. Reference should not be made to Framework policies that are not relevant to the prior approval matters.

5. Various terms are defined within the Classes themselves or under paragraph X of Part 3, if not within Article 2.

Limitations

6. Some Classes in Part 3 provide that development is not permitted where the site is on Article 2(3) land, in a SSSI, in a safety hazard area, a military

<!-- Part2 p.48 -->

explosives storage area, or if the building is a listed building or the building / site is or contains a scheduled monument31.

7. Various classes of PD in Part 3 are subject to limitations that the previous use of the building must have taken place for a specified period or on a specified date. In such cases, it must be established as a matter of fact on the evidence that the previous use was both subsisting and lawful. Consideration may need to be given as to whether the building had become divided into separate planning units, bearing in mind that – where relevant to the Part and Class – the term ‘building’ may mean ‘part of a building’, as defined in Article 1(2).

8. Using Class MA as an example, paragraph MA.1(1)(b) requires that the last “use of the building” fell within one or more of the classes specified in MA.1(2) for a continuous period of at least two years before the date of the application for prior approval. Thus, development is only permitted under Class MA if:

- The use of the whole building fell within one or more of the specified classes and the use was lawful,

- The part of the building subject to the proposed change of use could be deemed a separate planning unit, as a matter of fact and degree, and its use fell within one or more of the specified classes and was lawful.

9. If there is insufficient evidence to adjudge the planning unit, the appeal can be refused on this basis with reference to paragraph W.(3))b). The Enforcement ITM chapter provides advice on the ‘planning unit’.

Statement on the ‘Net Increase in Dwellinghouses’

10. Paragraph W.(2)(ba) requires that prior approval applications relating to Classes G, M, MA, N and Q (and, previously, O, P and PA) are accompanied by a statement specifying the net increase in dwellinghouses proposed. This does not apply to applications made on or before 5th April 201632.

11. The ‘net increase in dwellinghouses’ is the number of dwellinghouses proposed that is additional to the number on the site immediately prior to the development. Paragraph W.(2)(bb) sets out specific details required in the statement for development proposed under Class Q33.

### Curtilage

12. Classes A, G, H, I, L and M permit a change of use of a building only. Classes AA, MA, N, Q, R, S and T permit a change of use of a building and land within its curtilage; the same was true of Classes O, P and PA.

13. For Classes Q (before 21 May 2024), R and S, ‘curtilage’ is defined in paragraph X as ‘(i) the piece of land, whether enclosed or unenclosed, immediately beside or around the agricultural building, closely associated with

[^31]: The LPA should refuse any prior approval application where such restrictions apply. Information regarding a safety hazard area or military explosives storage area should be included in the LPA’s Questionnaire and noted as a health & safety issue for any site visit. The Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) (England) (Amendment) Order 2018/343 amended the Article 2(1) definition of “military explosives storage area”.

[^32]: SI 2016/332 as before

[^33]: The Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) (England) (Amendment) Order 2024/579

<!-- Part2 p.49 -->

and serving the purposes of the agricultural building, or (ii) an area of land immediately beside or around the agricultural building no larger than the land area occupied by the agricultural building, whichever is the lesser.’

14. Specific definitions of ‘curtilage’ were set out in paragraphs P.3 and PA.3 for the now expired Classes P and PA. Paragraph Q3.(1) sets out a specific definition for the purpose of Class Q from 21 May 2024. It should be clear on any relevant prior approval application as to which land is ‘curtilage’ and subject to the proposed change of use. If there is no such clear plan, the application should be treated as relating to the building only, noting that ‘any land’ can comprise ‘a building’ under s336(1) of the TCPA90.

15. The GPDO does not define curtilage for the purposes of Class AA, MA, N, O or T. In an Enforcement or prior approval appeal relating to such classes, and if the matter is in dispute, the curtilage should be considered on the basis of the common law definition as discussed in the Enforcement chapter.

16. If there is any dispute in relation to Class P, PA, Q, R or S, the extent of the curtilage should be considered in accordance with the statutory definition, that is, paragraph P.3, PA.3, Q3.(1) or X, as the case may be. The land must be ‘immediately beside or around the building’, and the effect of the text ‘whichever is the lesser’ is that development cannot be PD if it would involve the change of use of an area of land that is larger than the curtilage.

Curtilage: Change of Use of the Building only

17. It is open to an applicant to propose a change of use of the building, along with any associated conversion works, without requesting any change of use of the land within the curtilage of the building at all. The effect of this would be that the use of the building would change, but the surrounding land would remain in the previous use.

18. Any subsequent application for prior approval of the change of use of land to create a garden around the dwelling must relate to land that meets the relevant GPDO definition of curtilage. If the developer obtains prior approval for a change of use of a building (and land) to a dwellinghouse and then wishes to provide a larger garden, they would need to apply for express PP for a material change of use of land and such an application would be considered on its merits, that is, on a s38(6) basis.

19. There is no requirement for a development proposed under Part 3 to include a curtilage and so an appeal should not be dismissed simply because one is not shown within the red line of the site. An appeal can be determined within the terms of the Order and without the need for reference to a curtilage.

Curtilage: Building or Part of a Building

20. In cases where the prior approval application relates only to part(s) of a building, with other parts being demolished or not subject to the proposed change of use, the area to be considered as within the curtilage of the building for the purposes of paragraphs P, PA, Q3.(1) and X (where appropriate) should be strictly related to – that is, no larger than – the part of the building which is subject to the proposed change of use.

Curtilage: Excluded from the Site Edged Red and/or Unclear

<!-- Part2 p.50 -->

21. It may be apparent from the representations that the proposed development encompasses land within the curtilage of the building, although that is not shown within the site edged red. In such cases, prior approval can be granted if the extent of the curtilage and its compliance with the relevant definition can be identified from the papers overall.

22. If the curtilage would not comply with the relevant definition, or the developer has provided insufficient information to enable the Inspector to establish such compliance, the Inspector may:

- Dismiss the appeal with reference to paragraph W.(3) or

- Conclude that there is no curtilage and grant prior approval strictly for the change of use of the building or

- Define the curtilage and grant prior approval simply in respect of an area which meets the definition.

23. The key point is that prior approval can be granted in respect of land within the curtilage of the building only where the extent of the curtilage is or can be made clear and that curtilage would meet the relevant definition. It must be apparent which land is subject to the permitted change of use.

Curtilage: Different to Site Edged Red and/or Too Large

24. Whether or not it is clearly identified on a plan, the curtilage may differ from the site edged red. The correct approach remains to assess the area identified as curtilage against the relevant definition. The Inspector should state for the avoidance of doubt that prior approval is only granted, and the change of use is only permitted, in respect the curtilage shown on the plan.

25. If the proposed change of use would relate to an area that exceeds the relevant definition of curtilage, it is again open to the Inspector to consider whether prior approval could be granted in respect of a smaller curtilage or, if that cannot be reasonably established, to dismiss the appeal.

Curtilage: Proposed Access

26. Where it is proposed to create a new access to the building subject to the change of use, the point where the access would not be ‘immediately beside or around the building’ should be assessed on a fact and degree basis. It may be noted that:

- Any operational development required to construct or upgrade an access beyond the curtilage may be PD under Part 2, Class B, which permits the formation, laying out and construction of a means of access to a highway that is not a trunk road or classified road. The access would have to be ‘required’ to serve the dwelling but not restricted in length.

- However, the use of any land outside of the curtilage where a proposed access would be formed, or where an existing access which serves the existing lawful use would be utilised by the proposed dwelling, will remain in its existing lawful use. Any material change of use of the land to use for residential purposes would be liable to require a separate grant of PP.

### Classes M, N and Q – Building Works

<!-- Part2 p.51 -->

Types of Application

27. Classes M and N permit development consisting of (a) a change of use of a building or (b) a change of use together with building operations reasonably necessary to ‘convert’ the building. The same applies to Class Q prior to 21 May 2024 (and subject to transitional arrangements discussed below).

28. As amended from 21 May 2024, Class Q permits (a) a change of use of a building, (b) a change of use together with the extension of a building or (c) a change of use together with building operations reasonably necessary to convert the building or to extend that building. Notwithstanding the repetitions of "or", the PD right is likely to encompass building operations reasonably necessary to convert and/or extend the buildings.

29. Applications may still be made for prior approval under Classes M, N or Q in relation to a change of use only. Where prior approval is sought under these or any other Class in Part 3 for a change of use only, but building or other operations are nonetheless shown on the submitted plans, the Inspector should be clear that those works are outside of their remit. This applies even if it appears likely that the operations would be required to facilitate the change of use or meet any requirements of the GPDO such as the provision of natural light in all habitable rooms. The Inspector should state in Preliminary Matters that they cannot speculate either as to whether the works would require a separate grant of planning permission, or on the merits of the works.

30. W.(2)(a) states ‘the application must be accompanied by… a written description of the proposed development, which, in relation to development proposed under Class M, N or Q of this Part, must [in the same application] include any building or other operations’; emphasis added. No such information is required if no building or other operations are proposed.

31. Where applications are made for a change of use and associated operations as described under Class M(b), N(b), Q(b) or Q(c), the works should take place with the change of use. If an applicant applies for prior approval for a change of use only under Classes M(a), N(a) and Q(a), and later finds that works are required, they must submit a new prior approval application for the change of use plus operations before the development is commenced.

32. An Inspector can make a split decision on an application for a change of use plus works, so as to grant prior approval for the change of use alone. This applies even if some operations would be necessary, since they could be subject to a later application for express PP.

33. Taking an appeal made in respect of Class Q(c) (from 21 May 2024) as an example: if the Inspector is satisfied in respect of the change of use and the matters referred to in Q2.(1)(a) to (e) and (g), but they are not satisfied with the design or external appearance of the building (Q2.(1)(f)) as shown on the proposed plans, they can grant prior approval for the change of use only.

34. However, the appeal should be dismissed if the Inspector is not satisfied – or needs more information – in respect of the change of use and any of the associated prior approval matters referred to in Q2.(1)(a) to (e) and (g). In that situation, the Inspector would not need to consider the proposed works.

<!-- Part2 p.52 -->

35. If the LPA refuses a Class M, N or Q application on grounds relating to building operations when none had been proposed, but the appellant then submits information on works during the appeal process, the Inspector should still determine the appeal as though it relates to a change of use only. In the interests of openness and fairness, the appellant should be advised to make a further prior approval application for a change of use plus works.

36. Multiple prior approval applications can be made for the same building over time, subject to the relevant limitations for Classes M, N and Q.

Internal and Structural Alterations

37. Under s55(2)(a) of the TCPA90, development that requires PP does not include works of ‘maintenance, improvement or other alteration which affect only the interior…or do not materially affect the external appearance of the building’. The nature and extent of proposed building operations should be assessed – on a fact and degree basis – to inform a conclusion as to whether they would amount to development and require PP via the GPDO at all.

38. The nature and extent of works should also be assessed to inform a conclusion as to whether they would fall within the PD rights set out in Class M, N or Q, as the case may be. The operations should be ‘reasonably necessary’ to facilitate the permitted change of use and comply with the relevant limitations and conditions.

39. There is a difference in law between ‘maintenance’ and rebuilding34. If the operations would amount to rebuilding, PP will be required but not granted under Class M, N or Q. It was held in Hibbitt v SSCLG [2016] EWHC 2853 that the building must be capable of conversion to residential use without operations amounting to complete or substantial re-building of the pre-existing structure or, in effect, the creation of a new building; see also PPG paragraph ref ID: 13-105-20180615 for discussion on this issue in relation to Class Q.

40. In considering whether operations would be permitted under Class M, N or Q, the GPDO 2015 makes no distinction between structural and non-structural works. There is no restriction on whether works are structural or not, and the operations do not need to be demonstrably essential in order to be found 'reasonably necessary'. Even if other options would be open to the developer, the question for the decision maker is whether the course proposed is one that a reasonable person would choose on the balance of probabilities.

41. Once a permitted change of use has occurred under Classes M, N and Q – or indeed any other Class – the building may be altered internally without reliance on PD rights or other permission.

Floorspace

42. Given the definition of floorspace set out in Article 2(1) of the GPDO 2015, the term would include any existing mezzanines or additional storeys. However, an additional internal floor may be added to the building following an initial

[^34]: Street v Essex CC [1965] 193 E.G. 537; Larkin v Basildon DC [1980] JPL 407

<!-- Part2 p.53 -->

change of use under any other Class of Part 3 since the works would be unlikely to constitute ‘development’ under s55(2).

43. The amount of floorspace subject to the proposed change of use is limited under Class I, and limited on a cumulative basis under Class M, N or Q, as discussed in respect of each of those classes below. Prior approval may be refused for development under Class M, N or Q where the cumulative floorspace in the new use would exceed the relevant limitations.

44. However, the limitations are to the floorspace ‘of the existing building changing use’ and ‘not on the size of the building or buildings in which the change of use occurs’; Mansell v Tonbridge and Malling BC & others [2017] EWCA Civ 1314. This is because ‘the existing building’ in question must be read as potentially referring to ‘part of a building’ as set out in Article 2(1).

45. In other words, the change of use of part of the building is permitted under Class M, N and Q. It may be argued that the limitation on cumulative floorspace does not apply to a proposed development where a previous change of use under the same Class was previously granted prior approval in respect of a different part of the same building. The Inspector will need to look at the relationship between the previously approved and now proposed changes of use on a fact and degree basis.

46. There is a limitation to the gross floor space of the existing building subject to the PD right set out under Class PA; the same was true for the now expired PD right under Class P. However, Article 2(1) provides that the term ‘building’ does not include any part of a building for the purposes of Classes P or PA.

47. From 21 April 2021, paragraph W.(2)(bc) requires, in relation to Classes G, M, MA, N, O, PA or Q, the floor plan to indicate “the total floor space in square metres of each dwellinghouse” as well as the dimensions and proposed use of each room, the position and dimensions of windows, doors and walls, and the elevations of the dwellinghouses.

### Class A: Casino, Betting Office, Pay Day Loan Shop or Hot Food Takeaway to Commercial Business and Service

48. Development is permitted under Class A only for a change of use of a building

– not including land within the curtilage or any building operations.

49. Class A was amended in May 201635 and again on 1 August 202136 to change the scope of the PD right, with latter amendments being pursuant to those made to the UCO.
