In short, development is now permitted under Class A for a change of use from a use falling within Article 3(6)(m), (n), (o) or (r) of the UCO to a use falling within Class E of Schedule 2 to the UCO.

50. The PD right is subject to one condition, A.1, that the developer must provide written notification to the LPA, before beginning the development, of the date on which the use of the building will change.

53. Class G was amended on 1 August 2021 subject to savings and transitional arrangements39, largely pursuant to amendments to the UCO. Development is permitted for a change of use of a building (only):

(c) from a use within Article 3(6)(n) or (o) to a mixed use for any purpose within Class E plus up to 2 flats

### Class M: Certain Uses to Dwellinghouses

61. Class M was amended in April 201644 and again in August 202145 in respect of the uses from which a change to a dwellinghouse may be made. In summary, Class M now permits a change of use of a building (only) to a dwellinghouse from use as a launderette, betting office, pay day loan shop, hot food takeaway, or a mixed use combining a launderette, betting office or pay day loan shop with a dwellinghouse. Where there is a mixed use, it does not matter if permission was granted via Class G of Part 3.

62. Class M was amended on 6 April 201846 so as to permit (a) the change of use or (b) the change of use plus building operations that are reasonably necessary for the conversion. The PD right relates only to a building and not land within the curtilage.

63. Under M.1(e) and (f), development is not permitted if it would result in the external dimensions of the building being extended beyond those existing or consist of demolition other than partial demolition of the building to the extent that is reasonably necessary for the building to function as a dwelling. Otherwise, however, there are no express limitations on what building operations may be reasonably necessary.

64. Thus, operations involved in the excavation, installation or strengthening of foundations could be permitted. Such works would be likely to represent ‘development’ – subject to what works are proposed as a whole – and they could be described as reasonably necessary if, for example, they are required to support a replacement wall which is reasonably necessary.

65. However, if new or reinforced foundations are proposed simply to support the existing building – or the totality of works would amount to complete or substantial re-building as per Hibbitt (as discussed above) – the works may not be PD under Class M. Any structural evidence before you will be crucial, and your judgment should be made on a fact and degree basis.

66. Under paragraph M.1(a), development is not permitted if the building was not [lawfully] used for one of the purposes referred to in Class M(a) on 20 March 2013 or, if in use before that date but not on that date, when it was last in use.

67. Under Class M, the cumulative floorspace of the existing building (see above) subject to the change of use is limited but not the number of dwellings; M.1(c) and (d). The units created must fall within the definition of dwellinghouse – that is, they must be self-contained units of habitation.

68. Paragraph W.(2A) provides that prior approval must be refused if adequate natural light is not provided in all habitable rooms as defined in paragraph X.

69. From 6 April 2021, Article 3(9A) of the GPDO provides that Schedule 2 does not permit any new dwellinghouse where the gross internal floorspace is less than 37m2 or there is not compliance with the nationally described space standard issued by DCLG on 27 March 201548.

70. Under M.2(3)(c), where the proposed development includes a change of use from a use falling within what were use classes A1 or A2, the application for prior approval must have been made on or before 31 July 202149. After that, a change of use from shops etc to dwellinghouses is permitted under Class MA.

### Class P: Storage or Distribution Centres to Dwellinghouses

88. Development is permitted under Class P for a change of use of a building and land within its curtilage from a use falling within use class B8 to a use falling within use class C3. The term ‘curtilage’ is defined for the purposes of Class P in paragraph P.3.

89. Under paragraph P.1(a) and (b), development is not permitted if the building was not [lawfully] used solely for a storage and distribution use on 19 March 2014, or when last in use, and the building was not so used for a period of least four years before the date that development under Class P begins.

90. Since Class P only permits a change of use, and given the limited prior approval matters set out in P2.2.(b), court cases relating to conversion or rebuilding, such as Hibbitt, are not relevant to Class P prior approval applications. Any building works which amount to development will require express planning permission.

91. Class P is a temporary one; paragraph P.1(c) provides that development is not permitted if the prior approval date falls on or after 1 June 201960. Subsequent amendments to the GPDO in relation to natural light and space standards did not apply to Class P. The development must have been completed – under P.1(k) – within a period of three years starting with the prior approval date.

92. For the purposes of Class P, the term ‘building’ does not include ‘part of a building’; see Article 2(1)61. Under P.1(d), development is not permitted if the gross floor space of the existing building exceeds 500m2, and that must be taken as a limit to the size of the whole building. Class P previously permitted the change of use of up to 500m2 of a larger storage and distribution depot.

93. Since the term ‘gross’ floorspace is used in paragraph P.1(d), walls should be included in the measurements in accordance with the RICS Gross External Area. The measurement of gross floorspace should also include any communal residential areas, for example, lifts, stairs and corridors.

### Class PA: Premises in Light Industrial Use to Dwellinghouses

94. Class PA was added to the GPDO in April 201662 as another temporary PD right. Development is permitted under Class PA for a change of use of a building and land within its curtilage from a use falling within use class B1(c) – light industrial use – to a use falling within use class C3.

95. For the purposes of Class P, the term ‘building’ does not include ‘part of a building’; see Article 2(1)63. The term ‘curtilage’ is defined for the purposes of Class PA in paragraph PA.3.

96. Development is not permitted under Class PA if:

### Class Q: Agricultural Buildings to Dwellinghouses

The ‘Old’ and ‘New’ Class Q and Transitional Arrangements

99. The development permitted under Class Q and the limitations to such PD were significantly amended on 21 May 2024, when the Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) (England) (Amendment) Order 2024/579 comes into force.

100. Given the transitional arrangements set out under Article 10 of the amending Order, prior approval applications could be made in respect of the old Class Q up until the end of 20 May 2025. Inspectors needing to consider Class Q as it was before 21 May 2024 should consult the 1 August 2020 version of the GPDO 2015.

101. Where prior approval is sought in respect of the new Class Q, however, it does not matter when the application was made. As advised above, Inspectors must decide prior approval appeals with regard to the Order in force on the date of the decision unless transitional arrangements apply.

Limitations: ‘Old Class Q’ (to 21 May 2024, with transitional arrangements)

102. From 6 April 201865 to 21 May 2024, Class Q permitted development consisting of—

(a) a change of use of a building and any land within its curtilage from a use as an agricultural building to a use falling within Class C3 (dwellinghouses) of the Schedule to the Use Classes Order; or

(b) development referred to in paragraph (a) together with building operations reasonably necessary to convert the building referred to in paragraph (a) to a use falling within Class C3 (dwellinghouses) of that Schedule.

[^64]: SI 2020/632 and 2020/1243 as before

[^65]: SI 2018/343 as before

<!-- Part2 p.61 -->

103. The change of use permitted under the ‘old’ Class Q encompassed land within the curtilage of the building, with curtilage then being defined by Paragraph X of Part 3.

104. Under paragraph Q.1(a), development was not permitted by Class Q if the site was not used solely for an agricultural use as part of an established agricultural unit on 20 March 2013, or when last in use, or – if brought into use after 20 March 2013 – for a period of at least ten years before the date that development under Class Q begins. Points to note here are:

- The building must have been in use for agricultural purposes as well as part of an established agricultural unit on the relevant date.

- Where the site was in agricultural use on 20 March 2013, or when last in use, but the use then ceased before being resumed again later, Inspectors should follow advice on lawfulness above.

- The agricultural unit should not be confused with the planning unit.

105. Under limitation Q.1(g), development is not permitted under the old Class Q if development under Class A(a) or B(a) of Part 6 has been carried out on the established agricultural unit since 20 March 2013 or where development under Class Q begins after 20 March 2023, the period of ten years before the date it begins. This is to prevent PD rights under Part 6 being exercised to erect a building specifically for the purpose of later changing its use.

106. In terms of building operations, limitations Q.1(h) and (i) provide that development was not permitted if it would result in the external dimensions of the building extending beyond those existing, or consist of building operations other than the installation or replacement of windows, doors, roofs, or exterior walls, or water, drainage, electricity, gas or other services to the extent reasonably necessary for the building to function as a dwellinghouse; and partial demolition to the extent reasonably necessary to carry out those building operations.

107. The operations involved in excavating, installing or strengthening foundations are excluded from those permitted under paragraph Q.1(i).

108. The April 2018 amendments to Class Q included the introduction of the terms “larger” and “smaller dwellinghouses” as defined in paragraph Q.3. Development was not permitted under Class Q where:

Q.1(b): in the case of a larger dwellinghouse within an established agricultural unit, the cumulative number of separate larger dwellinghouses developed under Class Q exceeded three or the cumulative floor space of the existing building or buildings changing use to a larger dwellinghouse or dwellinghouses under Class Q exceeds 465 square metres;

Q.1(ba): the floor space of any dwellinghouse developed under Class Q having a use falling within Class C3 (dwellinghouses) of the Schedule to the Use Classes Order exceeds 465sqm66

[^66]: The Town and Country Planning (Permitted Development, Advertisement and Compensation Amendments) (England) Regulations 2019/907

<!-- Part2 p.62 -->

Q.1(c): in the case of a smaller dwellinghouse, within an established agricultural unit, the cumulative number of separate smaller dwellinghouses developed under Class Q exceeds 5; or the floor space of any one separate smaller dwellinghouse exceeds 100sqm;

Q.1(d): the development under Class Q (together with any previous development under Class Q) within an established agricultural unit would result in either or both of a larger dwellinghouse or larger dwellinghouses having more than 465sqmof floor space having a use falling within Class C3 or the cumulative number of separate dwellinghouses having a use falling within Class C3 exceeding 5.

109. It follows that development was permitted under Class Q – subject to one or a series of prior approval applications – for (b) and (ba) up to three larger dwellinghouses with a combined floorspace of 465m sqm, or (c) up to five smaller dwellinghouses each of which is no larger than 100smq, or (d) a mix of large and small homes with no more than three being larger, and there being no more than five altogether.

110. The effect of Q.1(ba) is that development was not permitted under Class Q if any single dwellinghouse would have more than 465sqm. However, the effect of Q.1(d) is that five could be permitted including one larger dwellinghouse with up to 465sqm floorspace, plus four “smaller” dwellings which each have up to 100m2 floorspace, creating 865sqm of residential floorspace on an agricultural unit. In calculating the number of new homes allowed, any existing homes within the established agricultural unit not granted permission under Class Q should be discounted; PPG paragraph ref ID: 13-104-20180615.

111. The matters set out under condition Q.2(1) include (g) the provision of adequate natural light in all habitable rooms of the dwellinghouse(s), which must, under Article 3(9A), have a gross internal floorspace of at least 37m2 and comply with the nationally described space standard67.

Limitations to ‘New Class Q’ (from 21 May 2024)

112. Class Q now permits development consisting of—

(a) a change of use of—(i) a building that is part of an established agricultural unit and any land within that building's curtilage, or (ii) a former

### agricultural building that was (but is no longer) part of an

established agricultural unit and any land within that building's curtilage, to a use falling within Class C3 (dwellinghouses)…

(b) development referred to in sub-paragraph (a) together with the extension of the building…or

(c) development referred to in sub-paragraph (a) together with building operations reasonably necessary to convert the building to a use falling within Class C3 (dwellinghouses)…or to extend that building.

113. The most significant changes to Class Q relate to what is permitted and the temporal limitations. Prior approval may be granted under Q.(a)(i) for a

[^67]: SI 2020/632 and 2020/1243 as before

<!-- Part2 p.63 -->

change of use of a building which is part of an established agricultural unit. It must be part of the established agricultural unit at the time of the prior approval application, and have been so on 24 July 2023 or for a period of at least ten years before the date that the Class Q development begins. However, it is not necessary in Q.(a)(i) cases for the building itself to be in agricultural use. Prior approval may be granted for the change of use of a building that was, for example, in non-agricultural use as part of a mixed use planning unit.

114. Prior approval may be granted under Q.(a)(ii) for the change of use of a former

agricultural building that was but is no longer part of an established agricultural unit. Limitation Q1.(b) provides that such development is not permitted if (i) the site was part of an established agricultural unit on 24 July 2023, Iii) if it ceased to be part of the established agricultural unit after that date and was not part of the established agricultural unit for a period of at least ten years before the date that the Class Q development begins or (iii) since ceasing the to be part of an established agricultural unit, the site has been used for any non-agricultural purposes. The upshot of Q1.(b)(iii) is that, while the building does not need to be in agricultural use or part of an established agricultural unit, it cannot have been put to any other use.

115. Another change from 21 May 2024 is that Class Q now permits a change of use under Qa(i) or (ii)…

(b) …together with the extension of the building…or

(c) …together with building operations reasonably necessary to convert the building to a use falling within Class C3 (dwellinghouses)…or to extend that building.

116. Class Q should be interpreted purposively and read as permitting building operations to both extend and convert the building. Prior approval appeals should not be determined on the basis that reasonably necessary conversion works would preclude the construction of an extension or vice versa.

117. Limitations to the size and design of any extension are set out under paragraphs Q1.(h)(i) and Q1.(i). Amongst other stipulations, an extension must be single storey, to the rear of the existing building and not sited on land that was previously covered by a hard surface.

118. Limitations to operations reasonably necessary to convert the building are set out under Q1.(h)(ii) and Q1.(j). Under Q1.(h)(ii), the developer may construct protrusions of up to 0.2m to accommodate works described in Q.1(j), which essentially replicate the old Class Q limitations discussed above. Such operations do not include excavating, installing or strengthening foundations. It is likely to be the case, however, that such works would be permitted for an extension or 20cm protrusion that meets the relevant limitations.

119. The limitations to Class Q have also been changed in respect of the number and size of dwellinghouses permitted, with the old references to ‘larger’ or ‘smaller’ dwellinghouses now removed. Development is not permitted if:

Q1.(c) the floorspace of any C3 dwellinghouse exceeds 150sqm.

Q1.(d): together with any previous development under Class Q within the original limits of an established agricultural unit [see paragraph Q3.(2] would

<!-- Part2 p.64 -->

result in the cumulative number of separate C3 dwellinghouses exceeding 10 or the cumulative floorspace of C3 dwellinghouses exceeding 1000sqm.

120. Thus, the new Class Q note permits – through one or a series of prior approval applications – more dwellinghouses with more cumulative floorspace than before via Q1.(d). None of the dwellinghouses, however, from 21 May 2024, may be larger than 150sqm under Q1.(c).

121. Under limitation Q1.(g), development is not permitted under the new Class Q if development under Class A(a) or B(a) of Part 6 has been carried out on the established agricultural unit during the period of ten years before the date development under Class Q begins.

122. There is no change to the condition imposed on Class Q, under Q2.(1) that, before beginning the development, the developer must apply to the LPA for a determination as to whether their prior approval will be required. There is no change to the prior approval matters relating to development permitted under Q(a) or Q(c). However, where the development proposed would include an extension permitted under Q(b), the developer must also apply to the LPA for a determination as to whether their PA will be required as to impact of the extension on the amenity of any adjoining premises.

123. However, a final change to note in relation to the new Class Q is that the term curtilage is now defined in paragraph Q3.(1) rather than Paragraph X, and ‘the original limits of an established agricultural unit’ are defined in paragraph Q3.(2). Within that phrase, the agricultural unit should be considered as above and still not confused with the planning unit.

Planning Policy and Guidance

124. PPG paragraphs ref ID: 13-104-20180615 to 13-109-20150305 relate to Class Q and advise in particular that: ‘Impractical reflects that the location and siting would “not be sensible or realistic”, and undesirable…that it would be “harmful or objectionable”…the location of the building…may be undesirable if it is adjacent to other uses such as intensive poultry farming buildings, silage storage or buildings with dangerous machines or chemicals’68.

125. Those PPG paragraphs are not yet updated in relation to the ‘new’ Class Q and therefore should be applied only where clearly still relevant. Where an extension is proposed, its ‘impact…on the amenity of any adjoining premises’ should be considered on a similar basis as in Part 1 or Part 20 appeals, with regard to matters such as overlooking, privacy and light; see, for example, PPG paragraph ref ID: 13-122-2021820.

126. Planning policy on green belts in the Framework is not relevant to Class Q, and nor are matters such as housing land supply, agricultural occupancy etc. Such issues should only be mentioned where it is necessary to say they are not relevant and given no weight; see the advice on the Framework above.

127. As per East Hertfordshire, judgments about prior approval matters should be framed by the context that this is not an application for express PP, but for the prior approval of development that is permitted by the GPDO for the purpose

[^68]: Following East Hertfordshire DC v SSCLG & Tepper [2017] EWHC 465 (Admin)

<!-- Part2 p.65 -->

of increasing the supply of housing. Planning judgment will be exercised against the backdrop of the purpose for creating this class in the first place.

### Class R: Agricultural Buildings to a Flexible Commercial Use

128. Class R was also amended from 21 May 2024 but not such that transitional arrangements are required69. Prior approval applications and appeals could be made before that date for development consisting of a change of use of a building and any land within its curtilage from a use as an agricultural building to a flexible use falling within one of the following: R(a) use class B8 (storage and distribution, (b) C1 (hotels) or (c) E (commercial, business or service.

129. From 21 May 2024, the permitted change of use is to a flexible use R(a) falling within one of (i) use class B2 (general industrial), B8, C1, E or F.2(c) (outdoor sport or recreation) or (b) for the provision of agricultural training.

130. While the change of use could be to a mix of uses all falling (say) within use class E, the PD right does not (either side of 21 May 2024) extend to a mix of uses between the use classes specified, or a mix of uses encompassing agricultural training.

131. The term ‘building’ may mean ‘part of a building’ for Class R, and the term ‘curtilage’ is defined in paragraph X of Part 3 for the purposes of this PD right.

132. Development is not permitted by Class R, under limitation R.1(a), either side of 21 May 2024, if the building was not used solely as an agricultural use as part of an established agricultural unit (i) on 3 July 2012, (ii) in the case of a building which was in use before that date, when it was last in use, or (iii) in the case of a building which was brought into use after 3 July 2012, for a period of at least 10 years before the development under Class R begins. In cases where (i) or (ii) applies, but agricultural use was resumed after 3 July 2012 after a period of cessation or other use, Inspectors should follow the approach set out in relation to lawfulness above.

133. Limitation R.1(b) limits the cumulative floorspace of buildings (or parts of buildings) changing use under Class R to 500sqm prior to 21 May 2014, and 1000sqm from that date. There are no restrictions within Class R relating to Article 1(5) land.

134. Condition R.2(a) provides that a site which has changed use under Class R may, subject to the prior approval procedure set out under R.3, subsequently change use to another use falling within one of the use classes comprising the flexible use. However, under R.2(b), once the use has been changed under Class R, the site is to be treated as having a ‘sui generis’ use rather one falling within a use class.

135. What that means is that – for example – if PD rights are exercised under Class R to change the use of the agricultural building to a use falling within use class E, the developer could subsequently use the Class R PD rights again to change the use of the building to one falling within use class C1.

[^69]: SI 2024/579 as before

However, the building would nonetheless be treated as having a sui generis use (rather than one within use class E or C1) so that:

- Any other change of use – even within (what would otherwise be) the same use class – would not be exempted from the definition of development set out under s55(2)(f), so that planning permission would be required and

- PP would not be granted via the GPDO because the PD rights set out under other classes of Part 3, such as Class MA (change of use of commercial, business and service uses falling within use class E to a use falling within use class C3) do not apply to the sui generis uses created under Class R.

136. Condition R.2(d) also restricts the uses that may take place where the change of use is to a use falling within use class B2 (from 21 May 2024).

137. Before changing the use of the site under Class R, and subsequently making any further change of use to one of the use classes comprising the flexible use, the developer must:

R.3(1)(a): provide specified information to the LPA where the cumulative floorspace of the building(s) changing use does not exceed 150sqm. The information required is unchanged from 21 May 2024.

R.3(1(b): apply to the LPA for a determination as to whether their prior approval will be required where the cumulative floorspace of the building(s) changing use does exceed 150sqm. The prior approval matters are unchanged from 21 May 224

138. Condition R.3(2) requires that, where the cumulative floorspace exceeds 150sqm and the prior approval procedure is required, the development is begun within a period of three years starting with the PA date.

## Annex C: Part 4 – Temporary Buildings and Uses

### Class A: Temporary buildings and structures

1. The size and means of construction of a building is highly relevant to Part 4, Class A PD rights; the larger and more permanent the building, the less likely it is to be genuinely ‘required temporarily’ in connection with the carrying out of development. It is for the appellant to show why the building is reasonably required. His or her intentions are relevant to that assessment but must be objectively assessed; R (oao Wilsdon) v FSS and Tewkesbury BC [2006] EWHC 2980 (Admin); [2007].

2. Where a building or structure is said to be ‘required temporarily’ in connection with operations, the operations themselves need to be lawful – as stated in paragraph A.1(b) – and to have commenced or be about to commence. It will be a matter of fact and degree as to whether the operations are continuing or can reasonably be held to have ceased at the time an enforcement notice was issued, such that the building or structure is in breach of condition A.2(a).

3. The tolerances for temporary uses in Part 4 do not apply when the intention is that the development should be permanent; Tidswell v SSE & Thurrock BC [1977] JPL 104. It will be for the appellant to show that the use was temporary, and the PD right was genuinely implemented.

4. Where an enforcement notice is upheld in respect of a caravan site, motocross, war games, market or other transitory use of land, on the basis that – on the facts – there is an intermittent permanent rather than a temporary use, and there is no Article 4(1) Direction in force, the developer can still implement PD rights. Again, it is for the developer to show that it is a genuine implementation of temporary use rights and not a recommencement of the prohibited permanent use71.

5. The developer could still utilise Part 4 rights even if there is no express saving in the requirements of the enforcement notice; Cord v SSE [1981] JPL 40. A notice cannot take away lawful use rights. Under s181(2), a notice can only require that an alleged use be discontinued permanently ‘to the extent that it is in contravention of Part III’. The implementation of a temporary use permitted under the Order (and thus in accordance with s60) is not in contravention of Part III of the Act.

6. In other words, while unlawful uses do not benefit from PD rights under Article 3(5)(b), this does not apply where the unlawful permanent use is carried out on a temporary basis in accordance with Part 4, Class B. The temporary use rights in Class B subsist alone and are not related to any other existing unlawful use.

7. The presence of permanent buildings and facilities, and changes to the character of the land may be relevant as to whether the proposed use is temporary within Part 4 or a permanent change of use – but only when the

[^71]: In that situation, s180(1) would apply such that the enforcement notice would cease to have effect so far as inconsistent with the permission for temporary use granted under Part 4.

<!-- Part2 p.69 -->

permanent building or changes would make it impossible to revert to the previous normal use between occasions when the new use occurs72.

8. If physical changes have occurred such that it would be impossible to revert to the previous normal use, a material change of use will have occurred from the previous use, even if the new use takes place on 28 days or less a year.

9. If physical changes take place which do not prevent the normal use from being carried out for most of the year, Part 4 Class B PD rights would apply to another use which does not take place for more than 28 days; Ramsay v SSETR & Suffolk Coastal DC (No. 2) [2002] EWCA Civ 118

### Class B: Temporary use of land

10. Class B provides that ‘the use of land for any purpose for not more than 28 days in total is PD, except in relation to the uses specified in Class B(a) and B(b), where the limit is 14 days. In considering whether either or both limits have been exceeded, it is appropriate to look at the planning unit and take into account the aggregate of the occurrence of different uses.

11. In a LDC appeal under s191, where uses undertaken were similar to B(b) uses but did not comply with the limitations in B.1(d), it was held that they could not be aggregated with permitted B(b) uses to claim activity in excess of 14 days in any one year over the necessary ten year period, such that the uses would be immune from enforcement action; Miles v NAW & Caerphilly CBC [2007] EWHC 10 (Admin).

### Class BA: Additional temporary use of the land during the relevant period

12. On 1 August 2020, given the Covid pandemic, Class BA was added to grant PD rights for temporary uses of land, in addition to the temporary PD rights set out in class B between 1 July and 31 December 202073. The “relevant period” set out in condition BA.2, following a subsequent amending order, is 1 January to 31 December 202174.

Class BB: Moveable structures for historic visitor attractions and listed pubs, restaurants etc.

13. On 16 April 2021, Class BB was added for temporary moveable structures75. It was originally a temporary right to run until 1 January 2022 but has since been made permanent76.

14. Before any moveable structure is provided under Class BB, the developer must apply to the LPA for determination as to whether prior approval will be required in relation to the siting and method by which it is to be installed. Conditions BB.3(5), (6) and (9) require the LPA to notify Historic England

## Annex D: Part 6 – Agriculture and Forestry

1 Advice in this and indeed the other Annexes applies to Enforcement and LDC appeals as much if not more than prior approval appeals. Any given paragraph may be relevant to Enforcement appeals but not prior approval appeals, or vice versa, or to both.

2 If there is a dispute as to whether development is permitted under Part 6, the first questions may be whether the site is ‘agricultural land’ and in an ‘agricultural unit’ as discussed in the main part of this chapter above. The next matter to establish is whether the development would be of the type permitted under Class A(a) and (b), or Class B(a) to (g).

3 From there, if you find that there is or would be a breach to a limitation to PD as set out in paragraphs A.1 or B.1; it would be appropriate to go straight to that point; Fayrewood Fish Farms Ltd v SSE & Hants CC [1984] JPL 267. It is only necessary for there to be failure on one limitation in Part 6 for development to be unlawful.

4 In such a situation, even if it is questioned as to whether the development would be ‘reasonably necessary for the purposes of agriculture’, the following text could be used: ‘Even if I were to accept that the development was reasonably necessary…it would not benefit from Part 6 because…’

5 It is critical to show clear and logical analysis of each test in Part 6, and conclude on each appropriate, particularly where the representations are less than adequate in identifying the correct criteria.

### Classes A & B: ‘reasonably necessary’

6 Classes A and B were amended from 21 May 2024 subject to transitional arrangements set out under Article 10 of the Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) (England) (Amendment) Order 2024/579.

7 For a building to be ‘reasonably necessary for the purposes of agriculture within that unit’, the structure itself and uses carried on within it must be reasonably necessary for the use of the land as an agricultural unit. The whole agricultural unit is the reference point.

8 There is no requirement that the building is intended to accommodate an existing agricultural activity, provided there is an agricultural use of the land and the building is reasonably required for agriculture; Jones v Stockport MBC [1984] JPL 274. The applicant is expected to demonstrate the need for the development.

9 The Inspector is not obliged to contemplate some possible but unlikely agricultural activity that is not suggested; Clarke v SSE [1993] JPL 32. However, he or she should consider what agricultural use the land might reasonably be put to and take account of more than the applicant’s intentions

– since they might change, or a future occupier might carry out different activities; Broughton v SSE [1992] JPL 550. The assessment can be based on future agricultural use, unlike that for ‘agricultural land’.

The ‘reasonably necessary’ assessment does not carry with it any connotation of profit or business viability. It also relates to the particular building on the

<!-- Part2 p.74 -->

particular unit, as defined at the time, and cannot be justified in terms of some future larger agricultural unit.

11 The size and nature of the unit may be crucial, as may be the nature of the proposed building. The size of the building, however, is unlikely to be a determinative factor; whether a smaller or simpler building would suffice would be a question of ‘absolutely’ rather than ‘reasonably’ necessary.

12 It was held in McKay & Walker v SSE & South Cambridgeshire DC [1989] JPL 590 that size was irrelevant in deciding whether a building was reasonably necessary because the Order permits agricultural buildings up to 465m2. However, the scale of engineering operations was held to be significant in Macpherson v SS for Scotland [1985] JPL 788.

### Class A: ‘of 5 hectares or more in area’

13 In measuring the agricultural unit, the extent of any dwelling (with its garden) or other building that is occupied for the purposes of farming by the person who occupies the unit, and the extent of any dwelling on the land that is occupied by a farm worker can be included; paragraph D.1.

14 However, if the development is to be carried out on a separate parcel of land which is less than 1ha in size, it is not PD; A.1(a). Even if it would be carried out on a parcel that is at least 1ha, that land must not include any dwellinghouse or garden, because it has to be on agricultural land.

15 Whether land forms a ‘separate parcel’ is a matter of fact and degree, but a substantial feature of separation would be necessary, e.g. a road rather than fences or hedges, for it to be regarded as a separate parcel; Hancock v SSE [1989] JPL 99; Tyack v SSE [1989] 1 WLR 1392.

### A.1(b): development under Part 3, Class Q or S

16 Development is not permitted under Part 6, Class A if it would consist of the erection or extension of any agricultural building on an established agricultural unit, as defined in Part 3, paragraph X, where development under Part 3, Class Q or Class S has been carried out in the period of ten years ending with the date on which the proposed Part 6, Class A(a) development begins.

17 The purpose of this limitation is plainly to ensure that PD rights are not exercised to change the use of buildings required for agriculture to dwellinghouses or schools. However, limitation A.1(b) does not mention Class R, suggesting that PD rights to erect or extend agricultural buildings can be exercised alongside PD rights to change the use of farm buildings to flexible commercial use.

### A.1(d): ‘not designed for agricultural purposes’

18 A building is ‘designed’ for the purpose for which its physical layout and appearance fit; Belmont Farm Ltd v MHLG [1962] 13 P&CR 417 DC. The importance of the building’s external appearance and layout was confirmed in McKay & Walker.

In Harding v SSE [1984] JPL 503, the Court accepted that ‘designed’ related to appearance and not function. However, the CoA later held in Clarke that

<!-- Part2 p.75 -->

‘designed for agricultural purposes’ was for the Inspector to decide as a matter of fact and degree.

20 It is necessary to consider appearance, layout and stated intentions, although more weight may be given to one factor than others. The test is whether the building is designed for the purposes of the agricultural activities which might reasonably be conducted on the unit.

### A.1(e): ‘ground area’

21 The limits to the size of floorspace permitted under Part 6, Class A were extended with effect from 6 April 2018 and 21 May 202485.

22 From 21 May 2024, limitation A.1(e) provides that development is not permitted if the ground area would be covered by:

(i) any works or structure (other than a fence) for accommodating livestock or any plant or machinery arising from engineering operations would exceed 1000sqm.

(ii) any building erected or extended or altered by virtue of Class A would exceed 1500sqm.

23 From 6 April 2018 to 21 May 2024, the limitation was 1000sqm in respect of

(i) or (ii). Prior to 6 April 2018, the limitation was 465sqm in respect of (i) or (ii). One thing that is unchanged is a requirement for the ground area to be calculated as described in Part 6, paragraph D.1(2)(a).

### A.1(i): accommodation of livestock or the storage or slurry or sewage sludge

24 This limitation applies to all works for accommodating livestock and is not limited to some form of habitation or shelter. A hard standing used for feeding sheep falls within that definition; Taylor v SSETR [2002] JPL 248.

25 Lang J held in R (oao Marshall) v East Dorset DC & Pitman [2018] EWHC 226 (Admin) that ‘Paragraph A.1(i) excludes from the scope of permitted development a proposed development ("the erection or construction of, or the carrying out of any works to, a building, structure or an excavation") which is used or to be used for the accommodation of livestock i.e. where accommodation of livestock is the purpose of the development’.

26 Lang J found that limitation A.1(i) must be distinguished from condition A.2(1)(a):

- Condition A.2(1)(a) prevents use of a development that has already been carried out as accommodation for livestock, but also recognises that there may be circumstances where such use of existing development would be legitimate “and so it provides for the exception in paragraph D.1(3)”.

- Paragraph D.1(3) cannot be read into paragraph A.1(i), which is not subject to the same exception as condition A.2(1)(a).

[^85]: SI 2018/343 and SI 2024/579 as before

### Appeal Ref: [] [Address]
