161. Weight should be attached to emerging local plans and their policies or allocations with regard to the factors set out in NPPF paragraph 49. The Inspector should also consider the prospects of an emerging plan being adopted within the period of any temporary permission that may be granted.

### ‘Large Scale Unauthorised Site[s]’

162. PPTS paragraph 12 states that: ‘In exceptional cases, where a local planning authority is burdened by a large-scale unauthorised site that has significantly increased their need, and their area is subject to strict and special planning constraints, then there is no assumption that [they are] required to plan to meet their Traveller site needs in full.’

163. At the time of introduction in August 2015, the Government stated that ‘…there is only one local authority caught in this position (Basildon District Council in respect of Dale Farm)’34. Since Dale Farm was an exceptional site with some 80 unauthorised pitches, Inspectors should take it that there is a high threshold for a ‘large scale unauthorised site’ to be a material consideration.

164. Moreover, the implications of any large scale unauthorised site for meeting Traveller site needs should be addressed at the local plan examination. If that

[^34]: Planning and Travellers: Proposed Changes to Planning Policy and Guidance: DCLG, August 2015

<!-- Part2 p.146 -->

has not happened since August 2015, perhaps because of when the development took place, it may be necessary to hear representations as to whether the unauthorised site is ‘large scale’ and, if so, to what extent the authority would be reasonably required to plan to meet their Traveller needs.

## Alternative Sites

165. Whether an appellant relies on general need, personal need or both, there is no requirement for them to prove a need to live specifically on the appeal site, or that no other site is available. The Court of Appeal held in South Cambridgeshire DC v SSCLG & Brown [2008] EWCA Civ 1010 that:

‘In seeking to determine the availability of alternative sites for residential Gypsy use, there is no requirement in planning policy, or case law, for an applicant to prove that no other sites are available or that particular needs could not be met from another site…such a level of proof would be practically impossible…’

166. Nonetheless, the appellant may have conducted an unsuccessful search, and there may be other evidence of the availability (or otherwise) of alternative sites, perhaps from the Council’s planning or housing records, a Strategic or site-specific FRA, Gypsy and Traveller liaison officers, site managers, estate agents, landowners or other Travellers. Any such evidence may assist in understanding the actuality of any need as well as availability on the ground.

167. Where there is some evidence of alternative pitches or sites, the Inspector will need to reach reasoned conclusions as to whether:

- The proposed occupiers could live on the alternative site lawfully, meaning that the residential use is subject to an extant planning permission or lawful development certificate, and the occupation of or numbers/types of caravans on the site would not be in breach of any condition(s).

- The alternative site is a genuine or realistic alternative, meaning suitable, affordable, available and acceptable as discussed below35 or whether dismissing the appeal would be likely to make the intended occupiers homeless, and lead to camping on unauthorised sites.

168. While the parties should have the opportunity to put forward their views, the subject of alternative sites will rarely need to be discussed in any depth. There are rarely any realistic alternative sites and that is not usually disputed.

### Suitability

169. To be considered realistic, alternative sites should be capable – in principle – of being used for residential purposes without causing unacceptable harm to the environment or community in conflict with the development plan, the NPPF or

[^35]: Doncaster MBC v FSS & Smith [2007] EWHC 1034 (Admin)

<!-- Part2 p.147 -->

PPTS. Suitability will also depend on whether any alternative site will meet the occupiers’ requirements in terms of size, characteristics and/or location.

170. The suitability of an alternative site will need to be compared to that of the site under appeal. Where the proposed site would include more than one pitch or plot to be occupied by named individuals – probably relying on personal circumstances – facts to be established should include:

- The relationships between the households, including any shared working or mutual care arrangements and how long they have lived/travelled together.

- How important it is for them to remain together and the consequences for them of living apart.

- Whether they could live apart on smaller sites close to each other36.

171. Similarly, it may be necessary to address whether and why the appellant requires a site that is large enough and includes suitable space for other uses, for example, the stabling of horses or storage of business equipment.

172. In terms of location, PPTS paragraph 25e) is clear that authorities should determine applications for sites from any Travellers and not just those with local connections. However, any requirement from the appellant to live in a particular area should be factored in when considering the suitability of any alternative sites. Relevant needs may include:

- Work related reasons for living in the area, such as road links or proximity to sources of work.

- Education or health-related reasons, such as children attending a particular school, or any occupier being treated at a local hospital.

- Proximity to family and/or friends in the area.

173. Land in commercial areas may be acceptable for travelling showpeople’s sites, given their needs to use, store and/or move plant, machinery and heavy vehicles, and the risk of such activities causing unacceptable noise or other pollution in predominantly residential areas. However, showpeople and their families will themselves require adequate living conditions. Alternative sites would need to be suitable for carrying out all uses in the mix.

### Affordability

174. The importance of affordability in relation to human rights was addressed in Chapman v UK [2001] ECHR 43:

[^36]: Moss v FSS & South Cambridgeshire DC [2003] EWHC 2781 (Admin)

<!-- Part2 p.148 -->

“The cost of a site compared with the applicant’s assets, and its location compared with the applicant’s desires are clearly relevant. Since how much the applicant has by way of assets, what outgoings need to be met by her, what locational requirements are essential for her and why they are essential are factors exclusively within the knowledge of the applicant, it is for the applicant to adduce evidence on these matters.”

175. It may be reasonable to ask how much was paid for a site, but detailed questions about assets and the affordability of another site would normally be unduly intrusive. In any event, the answers may be unreliable or not recordable without compromising data protection regulations.. It is usually more appropriate to focus questions on land prices in the area generally and whether there is a reasonable prospect of the appellant being able to afford another site.

### Availability and Acceptability

176. It may be necessary to adjudge whether an alternative site that is not yet available will become so and, if so, when. For example, it may be that an allocated site does not yet have planning permission, but the Council may be aware that the landowner is preparing an application which is expected to be submitted and approved within the following 12 months.

177. Where mooted alternative sites do not have planning permission, it may be necessary to assess whether their use as a Traveller site would probably be more, less or equally harmful than the appeal development in planning terms (given the Council’s reasons for refusal). If the alternative site is unlawfully developed and occupied already, the Council should be asked as to whether they intend to take enforcement action or what stage such action is at.

178. It is reasonable to ask the Council whether they know of any vacancies on existing public or private sites, the length of any waiting lists in respect of public sites, and the prospects of any pitches being rented to the appellant. In turn, the appellant may be asked if they have considered joining a waiting list.

179. However, the appellant may be unwilling to live on a Council site. Private sites are encouraged by PPTS and preferred by many Travellers, just as members of the settled community prefer to buy rather than rent. Living on a public rented caravan site can give rise to privacy or security challenges.

180. Pitches on private rented sites may also be unavailable or unacceptable to the appellant. Indeed, Travellers who own private sites tend to keep ‘vacant’ pitches for friends and family members, just as occupiers of bricks and mortar homes may not let out spare bedrooms. That said, PPTS paragraph 28b) encourages consideration being given to conditions which allow for temporary increases in caravan numbers on sites, to permit visitors – and potentially increase the letting of ‘spare’ pitches.

<!-- Part2 p.149 -->

181. Where the appellant seeks permission for what would be a strictly family-occupied site, a refusal to contemplate living with other people may carry limited weight if the appellant is homeless and alternative sites are available. Even then, however, the Inspector should be sensitive in dealing with the issue, bearing in mind that many Travellers have had distressing lived experience of being moved on by other landowners.

### Weighing the Options

182. It was held in Linfoot v SSCLG & Chorley BC [2012] EWHC 3514 (Admin) that the option of a temporary permission should not have been discounted on the basis that a change in planning circumstances would not occur when there was in fact a possibility of changes across the county. It may in some cases, depending on the evidence, be necessary to consider the likelihood of accommodation becoming available elsewhere.

183. However, Inspectors should not cast around for evidence of alternative sites across the country37. To repeat, the appellant does not need to demonstrate local connections, or that they must live on the appeal site, or that no other site is available. And their evidence does not have to be detailed or corroborated. The Inspector must adjudge the likelihood of homelessness if the appeal is dismissed and does not need to be ‘certain’ that there are no alternative sites38. The appellant’s case should be accepted if it is clear and there is nothing to suggest that it is probably wrong.

184. Those points are important because many Travellers have difficulties with reading and writing. Most land deals between Gypsies are by word of mouth and a handshake – which does not absolve them of the need to register details of the land transfer with the Land Registry but does mean they may well have less written evidence to provide.

185. Moreover, landowners and estate agents are unlikely to provide written statements of the non-availability of sites. Local authorities may not concede that there are problems on any public sites. There will rarely be documentary evidence of matters that might make it impossible for an appellant to move onto sites owned by other Travellers in the area.

186. Alternatives which are rarely realistic include:

- Staying on another site while the occupiers are travelling; this would be a temporary measure at best and potentially in breach of any ‘personal’ condition that the site is subject to.

[^37]: See also Beaver v SSCLG & South Cambridgeshire DC [2015] EWHC 1774 (Admin)

[^38]: Moore v SSCLG & Bromley LBC [2012] EWHC 3192 (Admin)

<!-- Part2 p.150 -->

- ‘Doubling-up’ on an existing pitch; this would likely be in breach of condition and/or result in overcrowding – although, .

- Moving into bricks and mortar housing; this may need to be explored39 but will often be contrary to the Traveller way of life and unaffordable. It is not uncommon to find that families have tried bricks and mortar accommodation before but, for a variety of reasons, found it unworkable.

- Moving onto a Park Home or static caravan site, where occupiers buy a caravan that is already on the land and pay a monthly rent to live there. Such sites are often subject to rules which set a minimum occupier age, and thereby occupied by older members of the settled community seeking affordable housing in retirement. These sites may also be subject to rules preventing the parking of touring caravans and/or the keeping of dogs.

187. However, an absence of alternative sites will not necessarily make it disproportionate to dismiss the appeal40.

## Policy Failure

188. It is sometimes argued that ‘policy failure’ – meaning failure of the local authority to provide Traveller sites through their planning policies – should be treated as a material consideration in favour of an appeal for a Traveller site. Whether that is the case and, if so, the weight attached to the consideration, will depend on the evidence and be for the judgment of the decision-maker.

189. There must be more to policy failure than giving a different name to any existing unmet need or shortfall on a five year supply of pitches or plots. For a claim to be supported, there must be evidence of a persistent failure of the authority to put policies or other measures in place to meet the accommodation needs of Travellers and of a corresponding long-standing unmet need for sites41.

190. As set out in Annex A, the CSCDA60 was designed to regulate and control private caravan sites. S23 of the Act gave local authorities the power to close common land to Gypsies and Travellers – and this led to a shortage of stopping places, despite local authorities being empowered under s24 to provide (compensatory) caravan sites.

191. Accordingly, s6 of the CSA68 imposed a duty on local authorities to provide sites for Gypsies. S6 was repealed by s80(1) of the CJPOA94 but that also amended by the CSCDA60 by inserting s24(2)(c) so that local authorities were

[^39]: R (oao Clarke) v SSTLR & Tunbridge Wells BC [2002] EWCA Civ 819

[^40]: Egan v SSTLR [2002] EWHC 389 (Admin)

[^41]: The report (5 April 2019) of the House of Commons Women and Equalities Select Committee inquiry into ‘Tackling inequalities faced by Gypsy, Roma and Traveller communities’ criticised a ‘persistent failure by both national and local policy-makers to tackle inequalities in any sustained way’, albeit with regard to policy issues other than those related to Traveller sites or encampments.

<!-- Part2 p.151 -->

empowered to provide sites specifically for Gypsies. Circular 1/94: Gypsy Sites and Planning (C1/94) made it clear that, after the repeal of the s6 duty:

“…planning authorities should continue to indicate the regard they have had to meeting Gypsies’ accommodation needs…in their development plans, through appropriate use of locational and/or criteria-based policies”.

192. Since C1/94, through C1/06: Planning for Gypsy and Traveller Caravan Sites and C4/07: Planning for Travelling Showpeople, PPTS 2012, PPTS 2015 and now PPTS 2024, local authorities have been continually required to plan to meet the accommodation needs of Travellers.

193. There may be scant information as to whether or how the authority has planned to meet Traveller needs, and how long there has been any backlog of need. However, if the appellant pursues a case based on policy failure, they may submit evidence in the form of historic development plan documents, GTAAs and/or appeal decisions.

## Personal Need and Circumstances

### Facts to (Try to) Establish

194. Personal need and circumstances are often pleaded in aid of Traveller site appeals – and were a key factor in the House of Lords’ judgment in South Buckinghamshire DC v SSTLR & Porter (No. 2) [2004] UKHL 33 to uphold an Inspector’s decision to grant planning permission subject to a personal condition for a Traveller site in the Green Belt. Where the appellant relies on personal considerations, it will be necessary for the Inspector to record the names of and relationships between the intended site occupants42.

195. In terms of personal need, Travellers generally need a settled base whether they travel for work or not. Those who still have a nomadic lifestyle need a base to which they can return during periods between work and join family members who do not travel in accordance with PPTS. To establish personal need, it is important to try and ascertain the relationships between the intended occupiers, their individual and collective needs, and whether any of them have anywhere else to live lawfully given:

- Where they are living now, if not on the appeal site.

- Whether they have ever had a settled base and, if so, why they left it, with regard to issues set out under ‘Alternative Sites’ above.

[^42]: Married women in Traveller communities may use their birth and married surnames interchangeably. Men may also have two surnames and a family group may have a ‘clan’ name.

<!-- Part2 p.152 -->

- Whether they can lawfully return to any other site as a whole family group (where appropriate) and without ‘doubling up’, otherwise giving rise to overcrowding or causing other unacceptable harm to living conditions.

- Whether they could live in bricks and mortar housing43. This question should be asked with sensitivity and not discussed at length. The answer in the vast majority of cases will be ‘no’ given the PPTS definition and Traveller’s cultural tradition of nomadism.

196. It may also be necessary to look at any personal circumstances which would add weight to the case for a grant of permission for their residential use of the appeal site, again having regard to the significance of any individual’s particular situation on the appellant group as a whole44, and indeed the Traveller tradition of living in extended family groups for mutual care and support.

197. Where occupiers on the site have ceased travelling ‘on grounds only of their own or their family’s or dependants’ educational or health needs or old age’, as per PPTS Annex 1, the appellant does not need to show that such needs are in some way ‘special’ in order for them to carry weight in favour of the appeal. However, it will be necessary for the appellant to describe the facts and circumstances that they wish to be considered, such as:

- Which occupiers, if any, have parental and/or caring responsibilities and which are ‘dependants’.

- The number and ages of any children, noting particularly any who are under 5 or of ‘school age’.

- Any adults who need particular support and/or are aged 65+.

- In the case of an extended family group, how long they have lived together or why they need to do so now.

198. Turning to education, it is usually necessary to assess in Traveller cases firstly the benefits of the child(ren) continuing or starting education from the appeal site and secondly the likely educational ramifications of a refusal of permission. It will be necessary to establish:

- How many children are currently enrolled at school.

- Whether the children are enrolled at primary and/or secondary school(s).

- How the children have settled at the school and any reasons for low attendance.

[^43]: R (oao Clarke) v SSTLR & Tunbridge Wells BC [2002] EWCA Civ 819

[^44]: Dartford BC v FSS & Lee [2004] EWHC 2549 (Admin)

<!-- Part2 p.153 -->

- Whether any children are on a register of special educational needs (SEN) or receiving any other special/extra help at school.

- The location of the school(s) and any local authority support needed for travel between the school and site.

- The children’s educational history: when they were first enrolled at school, any previous schools attended, any previous or continuing home schooling.

- What local educational support services for Traveller children exist, and what provisions they make for home-based learning.

- The consequences for the children’s education if the appeal is dismissed, with regard to the prospects or stage of enforcement action, the availability of alternative sites and the likelihood of the family living on the roadside.

199. Many children successfully change schools when their parents move home, but it is difficult for Traveller children to sustain attendance, if not even enrol at school if they have no fixed address or need to move between a series of temporary and/or unauthorised sites45. Children are likely to have lower educational attainment and experience other harm from the disruption if they miss school regularly or have to move between different schools46.

200. Inspectors should make reasoned findings47 on whether dismissing the appeal would be likely to render any children homeless, and the likely effects on their access to and stability of education. The weight attached to this consideration may be affected by factors such as the likelihood and degree of disturbance to education, the number of children involved, the strength of connection with existing school(s), and the transferability of any special help to another school.

201. It has been accepted that educational needs can carry significant (or more) weight even when they are not special or unusual48, as well as when there are special educational needs49. But even then, and if there is no realistic alternative site, the balance may still be against the appellant if sufficient harm is or would be caused by the development50.

202. Inspectors have granted temporary permission where a clear end point could be identified for what were decisive educational needs. However, most appeals relate to Traveller families with adult women of child-bearing age and/or

[^45]: Notwithstanding that s13(1) of the Education Act 1996 imposes on local authorities a general responsibility to make primary, secondary and further education available to meet the needs of the population of their area. It was held in Hughes v FSS & South Bedfordshire DC [2006] EWCA Civ 838 that ‘it is safe to assume that the Inspector was well aware of the local authority's obligations under the Education Act 1996 to make provision for the education of children in its area.’

[^46]: “A change of home, carer, social worker or school almost always carries some risk to a child’s development and welfare”, paragraph 1.6 of the Children Act 1989: Guidance and Regulations Volume 2 (June 2015)

[^47]: Coyle & Others v SSCLG & Basildon DC [2008] EWHC 2878 (Admin)

[^48]: Basildon DC v SSETR & Others [2000] CO/3315/2000 (HC)

[^49]: Dartford BC v FSS & Lee [2004] EWHC 2549 (Admin)

[^50]: Doran v SSCLG [2010] EWCA Civ 1798

<!-- Part2 p.154 -->

children of different ages, meaning it cannot be assumed educational needs will change within the timescale of temporary permission. It would normally be necessary to consider whether a grant of personal permission is justified.

203. Traveller communities have worse health outcomes than the population as a whole51. In 2006, it was recorded that Traveller life expectancy is lower by ten years for men and 12 years for women compared to the settled population; 42% of Travellers had a limiting long-term illness compared to 18% for the settled population; 18% of Traveller mothers had experienced the death of a child, compared to less than 1% of settled mothers52 53.

204. Since sick, disabled or elderly Travellers are cared for by their families, it is not unusual for health matters to be raised in Traveller appeals. Since there is a public health interest in universal access to basic health care, it will be necessary to establish in each case:

- Whether the intended site occupants are registered with a GP, the location of the practice and how it is or would be accessed from the site.

- If applicable, why the occupiers are not registered with a [local] GP54.

- Whether any intended occupants have health problems and, if so, the effects or limitations of these conditions55.

- Whether any intended occupants are receiving regular treatment from a GP, clinic or hospital and the frequency and location of appointments.

- Whether any occupiers require full or part-time care from another occupier or relative living close to the site.

205. As with education, it is usually necessary to establish the benefits for the individuals involved of being allowed to stay on the site compared to the consequences of a dismissal of the appeal – in terms of routine health care and/or particular health problems or caring needs, and with regard to the

[^51]: Health Status of Gypsies and Travellers in England, University of Sheffield o/b the Department of Health, 2004; The House of Commons Women and Equalities Select Committee inquiry into ‘Tackling inequalities faced by Gypsy, Roma and Traveller communities also reported on 5 April 2019 that ‘Gypsy , Roma and Traveller people have the worst outcomes of any ethnic group across a huge range of areas, including education, health, employment, criminal justice and hate crime’.

[^52]: Annex A (Race Equality Impact Assessment) to the Explanatory Memorandum to the Housing (Assessment of Accommodation Needs) (Meaning of Gypsies and Travellers) England Regulations 2006 (SI 2006/3190).

[^53]: Overcrowding can be a major problem on many travelling showpeople’s sites from family growth and larger sized equipment, but this community does not appear to have the same concentrations of major health problems and high morbidity as there are amongst Gypsies and Travellers.

[^54]: The then Secretary of State for Health, Jeremy Hunt confirmed in a letter of 26 March 2015 to Friends, Families and Travellers that GP practices cannot refuse an application to join its list of NHS patients on the grounds of race, gender, social class, age, religion, sexual orientation, appearance, disability or medical condition, and there is no requirement for an applicant to have a permanent address or a provide identification when registering with a GP.

[^55]: Bearing in mind that the definition of disability in s6 of the Equality Act 2010 focusses not on the diagnosis but on the effect of the ‘impairment’ on ability to carry out normal day-to-day activities.

<!-- Part2 p.155 -->

availability of alternative sites and, if the occupiers are already living on the appeal site, the prospects or stage of enforcement action.

206. If no alternative, available and affordable site has been identified, and it is clear that conventional housing would be unacceptable56, then it is likely that dismissing the appeal would render the occupiers homeless – and that may make it difficult for the occupiers to access routine and/or specialist healthcare on a consistent basis, to access fresh water, sanitation and washing facilities, and/or to stay together and sustain caring responsibilities. It may lead to frequent moves from various unauthorised sites, and thus a lifestyle which is inherently insecure and physically demanding.

207. As with education, health problems or caring needs do not have to be ‘special’ to be given significant weight, but that is not to say they will. Acute or unusual problems or needs may attract additional weight.

### Dealing with People: Issues when Hearing Evidence

208. Where personal circumstances are raised, it is helpful – though not always crucial – if documentary evidence is provided from appropriate professionals. The authority should be asked if they accept the contents of such material.

209. At hearings or inquiries, appellants and witnesses may agree to be cross examined or asked questions. As in any other casework, Inspectors should be alert to the inherent sensitivities in dealing with personal circumstances and consider whether, or the extent to which it is necessary for such details to be aired orally in public. Questions and discussion should be limited to the minimum needed in order to understand and assess the implications of their circumstances for the appeal decision.

210. Intrusive questioning of the appellant or others should be curtailed, whether in respect of personal matters or the Traveller way of life, including that Travellers live and work in family groups; care for the elderly, sick or disabled members within the family; and require particular sanitation facilities. If necessary, clarify these traditions for the benefit of settled persons who are interested parties.

211. The Inspector should ensure that any person with difficulties in reading and writing is able to fully participate in the hearing or inquiry, by giving clarifications throughout the event and by giving any agent time to talk them through documents. If appropriate, the Inspector can explain to the parties that giving the individual time and assistance is necessary to ensure that proceedings are fair and to obtain the evidence needed to make the decision.

[^56]: R (oao Clarke) v SSTLR & Tunbridge Wells BC [2002] EWCA Civ 819

<!-- Part2 p.156 -->

### Dealing with Information: Data Protection

212. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), brought into UK law through the Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA18), prohibits (subject to exemptions), the processing (which includes the dissemination or otherwise making available) of special categories of personal data, being that which reveals

The racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs or trade union membership [of an identifiable living individual]; genetic or biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person; or data concerning a natural person’s sex life or sexual orientation57.

213. Personal data relating to health should be treated as subject to Article 9(1) even if it is not strictly ‘genetic or biometric’ in nature.

214. An exception to that prohibition applies where the processing of the personal data is necessary for reasons of substantial public interest. It will be for the Inspector to consider the extent to which there is a substantial public interest in disseminating or otherwise making available any personal data within the special categories – or indeed any other sensitive personal information.

215. It is accepted that some personal data is likely to be more sensitive, based on the potential harm or impact on the individual(s). Information relating to children, including their name, age, address or school is likely to be seen to be more intrusive than that relating to an adult. Inspectors must be alert to the risk of hate crime against Travellers, whether or not they are or are not perceived to be ethnic Romani Gypsies or Irish Travellers.

216. Hearings and inquiries, as public events, must be conducted to avoid the publication of special categories of personal data or other sensitive personal information. The Inspector may require that any filming or recording of a hearing or inquiry is paused when any personal matters are to be described in evidence or submissions.

217. Full advice on writing decisions to enable publication which does not contravene data protection regulations is set out in Annex 5 of the Approach to Decision Making ITM chapter.

## PPTS Status

218. It is not unknown for authorities to cite lack of PPTS status as a reason for refusing a Traveller site application. However, planning permission normally runs with the land and so the first question is whether the use of land as a residential caravan site for occupation by Gypsies or Traveller is acceptable in planning terms, with the identity of the occupiers liable to change.

[^57]: Article 10 of the UK GDPR does not prohibit but sets out strict limitations to the processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions or offences, or related security measures.

<!-- Part2 p.157 -->

219. It is not necessary for an individual to have PPTS status in order to seek or be granted planning permission for a Traveller site. The application – which may even be made by an organisation rather than person – should be considered on the basis of its description58. Where permission is granted for the use that complies with local plan policies relating to Traveller sites and/or PPTS, a condition should be imposed to restrict occupation to persons with PPTS status.

220. In some cases, imposing such a condition might mean that the appellant or intended occupiers could not lawfully live on the land, but that should not a reason to refuse the appeal. The appellant could, after all, sell the site with the benefit of the permission. In the event that the appellant or others without PPTS status do move onto the site, the local authority would be able to take enforcement action against a breach of the relevant condition.

221. Some appeals may relate to family groups including people with and without PPTS status. The development should be considered on the basis that PPTS is applicable because matters such as the need for and supply of Traveller sites are likely to be relevant. However, it may also be necessary to enquire as to the relationships between members of the group, including whether any occupiers are dependents and the need for the family to stay together59. If permission is granted, it may be subject to PPTS occupancy and personal conditions.

222. Generally, then, if the use is acceptable on its merits, the question of status is likely to be immaterial. The exception is where the case for permission rests in whole or part on the personal circumstances of an individual or whole family without PPTS status. Such persons cannot benefit from any policies aimed at providing for Travellers. The question would then be whether to grant planning permission for a residential caravan site on the basis of the development plan, with regard to the NPPF and the occupiers’ rights under Article 8.

223. Since Gypsies and Travellers are defined in PPTS Annex 1 as including persons with a cultural tradition of nomadism, ethnic Gypsies and Travellers intending to live on a proposed Traveller site can now be expected to have PPTS status, even if they have never travelled or ceased travelling for reasons unrelated to education, health or old age. Evidence from the appellants relating to their ethnicity should be accepted unless it is credibly disputed.

### Facts to (Try to) Establish

224. Until December 2024, PPTS Annex 1 required that consideration is given to specified ‘issues amongst other relevant matters’ to take into account when

[^58]: Hearne v SSW & Carmarthenshire CC [1999] EWHC 494 (Admin), [2000] JPL 161 (Court of Appeal); South Cambridgeshire DC v FSS & McCarthy & O’Rourke [2004] EWHC 2933 (Admin)

[^59]: The House of Lords defined ‘dependants’ as persons living in family with the person defined and dependent on him (or her) in whole or in part for their subsistence and support; Fawcett Properties Ltd v Buckingham CC [1961] AC 636. It was held in Shortt v SSCLG [2015] EWCA Civ 1192 that, as a matter of ordinary language, ‘dependants’ may refer to relationships without financial dependency.

<!-- Part2 p.158 -->

considering PPTS status. That text is now deleted but, if PPTS status is in dispute, the questions would be likely to revolve around the phrase ‘nomadic habit of life’ – adjudged on a fact and degree basis60 – as before.

225. A ‘nomadic habit of life’ must have an economic purpose. The Court of Appeal held in R v South Hams DC ex parte Gibb [1994] QB 158 that, for the purposes of the CSA68, Gypsies are ‘persons who wandered or travelled for…making or seeking their livelihood…not…persons who moved from place to place without any connection between their movement and means of livelihood’.

226. Living away in a caravan from time to time for work, akin to a builder, may be insufficient to establish PPTS status61. However, travelling for work does not need to be the main or primary source of family income; trading at horse fairs for up to two months of the year can maintain status, so long as it has an economic purpose and is more than a hobby62. Travelling can be undertaken seasonally with regular return(s) to the settled base for part of the year63.

227. The relevant time as to when the appellant or occupier(s) have PPTS status is the date of the decision64 although their previous lifestyle is relevant. Questions to be asked may include:

- What kind of paid work is carried out by the occupiers.

- Patterns of travelling for work – and whether these have changed or would change on living on the site.

- Whether the occupiers own any horses and, if so, whether they are kept as a hobby or for breeding and/or trading.

- Where they (would) keep their horses, and if they own or rent that land.

- Whether they go to fairs to buy or sell horses or to trade in another respect.

- Whether any occupiers have ceased travelling (temporarily or permanently) and, if so, for what reasons.

228. Some members of a family or group may travel more than others; working age men typically travel routinely, but women, children and disabled or older men tend to travel less often, perhaps only for holidays. If there is a dispute over PPTS status, Inspectors should investigate the extent to which each occupier

[^60]: See Annex B, and particularly Wrexham v NAW & Berry [2003] EWCA Civ 835 or Medhurst v SSCLG [2012] EWHC 3576 (Admin), [2012] JPL 598.

[^61]: Clarke-Gowan v SSTLR & North Wiltshire DC [2002] EWHC 1284 (Admin)

[^62]: Maidstone BC v SSE & Dunn [1995] HC CO/2349/94

[^63]: Greenwich LBC v Powell [1989] 1 AC 995, (1989) 57 P&CR 49 (UKHL)

[^64]: Hearne v SSW & Carmarthenshire CC [1999] EWHC 494 (Admin); [2000] JPL 161 (CoA); it may be irrelevant if the appellants would start leading a nomadic lifestyle if and when the appeal is dismissed.

<!-- Part2 p.159 -->

travels, the reasons for not travelling65 and/or plans to resume travelling where applicable and the relationships between the individuals.

229. To repeat, however, the PPTS definition now encompasses a) persons of a nomadic habit of life who have ceased travelling permanently on specified grounds and b) persons with a cultural tradition of nomadism or living in a caravan. The latter group may include, for example, one who took on caring responsibilities upon leaving education. There is no requirement that such persons must have, or have had, or will have a nomadic habit of life.

230. Local authorities do not often challenge whether Travelling Showpeople meet the PPTS definition since most are members of the Showmen’s Guild of Great Britain. A regional representative of that organisation will often make written representations and/or attend the hearing/inquiry to support the appellant and provide an overview on need and whether there are realistic alternative sites.

## The Planning Balance

231. The overall conclusion in Traveller appeals will normally involve carrying out a balancing exercise in the usual way, starting with the planning balance before carrying out any human rights and/or equality assessments.

232. Set out the findings on each of the main issues, including the weight attached to each harm or benefit of the development with regard to conditions that could be imposed to mitigate the harm and/or ensure the benefits. If and where appropriate, the possibility of making a split decision should also be addressed.

233. As advised above, the decision should be made in accordance with s38(6) and with regard to material considerations including PPTS paragraph 28 and the application of NPPF paragraph 11d) where the local planning authority cannot demonstrate a five year supply of deliverable Traveller sites.

234. If the Inspector decides to not grant permanent permission, it will be necessary to undertake a second balancing exercise as to whether a grant of a temporary and/or personal permission would be justified given:

- Any harm to the Green Belt would still carry substantial weight although it should also be recorded that the duration of such harm would be reduced.

- Whether the limited period of the permission would overcome or result in reduced harm in respect of other matters, perhaps in respect of the character of the area or, given current rather than future risk, flooding.

- Whether conditions would be necessary to mitigate even temporary harm or to secure benefits still needed to justify the temporary permission and, if

[^65]: R (oao Massey & Others) v SSCLG [2008] EWHC 3353 (Admin), paragraph 23.

<!-- Part2 p.160 -->

so, whether it would be reasonable to impose such conditions given the cost of any works and the limited period of the permission.

- Whether there is a reasonable expectation of a change in planning circumstances, particularly in relation to any unmet need and the five year supply of deliverable sites (through the local plan process or otherwise) within what could be the period of a temporary permission.

- What would happen to the occupiers if the appeal is dismissed66 and whether their personal need or circumstances would tip the balance towards a grant of personal or temporary permission.

## Human Rights and Equality in Traveller Casework

235. Rights set out under the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA98) and the Public Sector Equality Duty (PSED) set out under the Equality Act 2010 are frequently engaged in Traveller casework. Comprehensive advice on upholding human rights and complying with the PSED is set out in the Human Rights and Equality ITM Chapter and not duplicated here67. The only additional points to stress here are that:

- For the purposes of Article 8, the “private and family life” of a Traveller encompasses living in accordance with their Gypsy or Traveller heritage, including living in a caravan, and a Traveller pitch or plot is a “home”.

- The best interests of the child(ren) – being those under 18 years old, even if they have left education or started work – is relevant to Article 8.

- For the purposes of the PSED, Romani Gypsies68 and Irish Travellers69 are ethnic minorities and thus have the protected characteristic of race under s149(7) of the EA10, whether they have PPTS status or not.

- The appellant and/or occupiers may have other relevant protected characteristics, such as age, disability, pregnancy/maternity and/or sex.

- The Article 8 rights and/or protected characteristics of interested parties may also be engaged in a Traveller case.

- Where engaged, irrespective of whether the occupiers have PPTS status, human rights and the PSED must be dealt with as an integral part of the reasoning that leads to the final decision. The Inspector should address, in their Conclusion to the decision letter, whether their decision to grant or

[^66]: Moore v SSCLG & Bromley LBC [2012] EWHC 3192 (Admin)

[^67]: See also PPG paragraph 21b-028-20150901.

[^68]: CRE v Dutton [1988] EWCA Civ 17

[^69]: O’Leary v Allied Domecq [2000] (unreported) 29 August 2000 (Case No CL 950275–79), Central London County Court, Goldstein HHJ

<!-- Part2 p.161 -->

refuse planning permission would lead to a disproportionate interference with any affected persons’ human rights and/or conflict with the PSED.

- To carry out that assessment properly, Inspectors should identify and address the main issues with regard to where or how human rights or the PSED may be engaged.

- For the purposes of Article 8(1), issues such as flood risk, highway safety, living conditions and general need for Traveller sites can bear just as much as personal circumstances on someone’s right to a private and family life and home.

- For the purposes of Article 8(2), “public safety” can include highway safety and flood risk issues, while “the economic well-being of the country” and “rights and freedoms of others” encompass the protection of the environment and thus a huge range of planning interests.

- Any unlawful use of the site can be relevant to the final balance70, not least given the Government’s policy regarding intentional unauthorised development. However, the occupiers’ personal need for a site and personal circumstances should be assessed and weighed separately.

- Personal circumstances may be decisive, bearing in mind matters such as:

o The needs of the children, including but not limited to their needs for a home, education, health care and stability in those regards;

o Any need for the site occupiers to live with or close to, and perhaps care or be cared for by members of their extended family;

o The duty to facilitate the Traveller way of life71, the importance of a settled base, any additional factors – such an adjacent paddock for keeping horses – relevant to the cultural traditions of the occupiers .

o The practical consequences for the individuals concerned if the appeal is dismissed, or even if permission is granted on a time-limited basis. Where an enforcement notice is issued, regard should be had to the timescales in relation to any enforced departure and to the time that may be necessary to look for alternative accommodation72 73.

- The weight attached to any finding is for the decision-maker given the evidence before them and current law and policy. No other consideration

[^70]: Chapman v UK [2001] ECHR 43

[^71]: Chapman v UK [2001] ECHR

[^72]: There can never be any guarantee of finding an alternative site.

[^73]: Even if there is no appeal on ground (g), an Inspector may exercise their powers of variation under s176(1)(b) to extend the time for compliance if there would be no injustice to the LPA or appellant. Any option of granting temporary planning permission via ground (a) should be considered first, not least so that conditions can be imposed, including to limit the number of caravans on the land.

<!-- Part2 p.162 -->

can be inherently more important than the best interests of the child, but the weight given to any consideration will depend on all of the circumstances in the case74.

- The potential to impose any reasonable and necessary conditions, including temporary or personal conditions, is also crucial to the human rights assessment. A grant of conditional permission can protect the public interest by means which interfere less with an individual's rights than an refusal of permission.

236. Inspectors should also be particularly mindful of Article 6 (the right to a fair trial or hearing) in Traveller casework. Again, this is discussed fully in in the Human Rights and Equality ITM Chapter but extra care may be needed in Traveller cases to avoid barriers to participation which are difficult or impossible for the parties or participants to surmount.

237. If, for example, the appellant lacks financial resources to make their case, an Inspector may take a positive step to adjourn the inquiry so that the appellant can apply for public funding for representation – so long as this would not lead to unreasonable delay75.

238. Likewise, if it appears that the appellant or others may not have the literacy skills needed to participate on a level playing field, the Inspector should seek to establish – sensitively – whether that is the case, and what assistance may be required at an early stage of the hearing or inquiry.

239. Any representative, friends or relatives of the appellant or occupiers may be able to help, but, even then, it may be necessary for the Inspector to read out documents and/or make other adjustments to proceedings. The Inspector should ascertain that the persons understand and agree the contents of any written statements submitted on their behalf.

## Temporary and Personal Conditions

240. When considering an appeal for a change of use of land for a Traveller or Travelling Showpeople’s site, appellants will often ask for a grant of permission on a permanent basis in the first instance or, failing that, a time-limited basis. Even if the appellant does not make that point, the Inspector should address the possibility of granting a temporary or personal permission for the site76.

241. As with any other casework, most Traveller appeals will be dismissed or allowed on a permanent basis. Where the latter outcome would be

[^74]: ZH (Tanzania) v SSHD [2011] UKSC 4

[^75]: A costs application may be made even if an Inspector allows such an adjournment.

[^76]: R (oao Jordan) v SSCLG & Thurrock BC [2008] EWHC 3307 (Admin)

<!-- Part2 p.163 -->

unacceptable77 but there are considerations in favour of the appeal, and the planning balance would change if the development is time-limited, there is the option of granting a temporary or personal permission.

242. The weight attached to all considerations should be revisited when the question is whether to allow the development on a time-limited basis. In Moore v SSCLG [2013] EWCA Civ 1194, the Inspector concluded against a grant of permanent and then temporary permission. In considering the latter, they gave increased weight to unmet need and reduced harm to the Green Belt, but did not reconsider the weight attached to visual harm or personal circumstances, or make clear findings as to what would happen to the appellant.

243. The Court of Appeal held that there was ample material before the Inspector on which to make a finding on the likelihood of roadside camping if permission was refused – and it was likely on the facts. That was important to the ‘harm’ side of the balance as well human rights considerations; the Inspector had recognised that roadside camping would probably be equally harmful to the Green Belt and potentially more harmful to the countryside than the appeal development.

244. The Court of Appeal thus held that:

“…the grant of temporary permission would still result in the harm identified by the inspector, and it may not be strictly accurate to describe that harm as being cancelled out or neutralised by the harm that would result from the refusal of temporary permission, but the overall balance would necessarily be affected if the harm resulting from the refusal of temporary permission would be equal to or greater than the harm resulting from…such permission.

“…it is far from inevitable that the Inspector would have reached the same conclusion if [they] had made a finding on the likelihood of roadside camping and followed through its implications…[the] refusal of temporary planning permission was [not] a reasonable reflection of the factors [the Inspector] was required to take into account in that context”.

245. In Ward v SSLUHC [2024] EWHC 676 (Admin), an Inspector’s decisions to refuse permanent and temporary planning permission for a Traveller site in the Green Belt were upheld; the Court found that the Inspector considered all the relevant factors and reached rational conclusions that were clearly open to them. However, that judgment again reinforces that, when considering whether to grant temporary (and/or personal) permission, Inspectors should consider the harms and benefits in the light of the duration of the development and a realistic assessment of what will happen to the site occupiers.

246. It will always be necessary to explain why a temporary condition is to be imposed and why it will last for whatever period is specified. There should be a

[^77]: If the development would be acceptable at the date of the decision, permanent permission should be granted even if it appears that alternative and possibly more suitable sites will be available in the future; Doncaster MBC v FSS [2007] EWHC 1034 (Admin); Clee v FSS [2008] EWHC 117 (Admin).

<!-- Part2 p.164 -->

realistic prospect that by the end of that period the circumstances will have changed. If there is no realistic prospect of that, the appeal should be dismissed, or permission should be granted on a permanent or personal basis78. As noted above, account may need to be taken of anticipated changes in the circumstances across a wider area than just that of the local authority79.

247. The PPG states that circumstances where a temporary permission may be appropriate include where it is expected that the planning circumstances will change in a particular way at the end of that period80. Regard should be had to the likelihood of any change that may occur during the potential timescale of a temporary permission in respect of any of the main issues for the appeal, particularly in respect of the supply and availability of sites. Changes that may be anticipated can include the adoption of an emerging plan.

248. The period of the temporary condition will depend upon the circumstances of the case, but often depends on when alternative sites seem likely to become available. Relatively few temporary permissions have been granted for more than three years, but a longer period may occasionally be justified.

249. The PPG allows that permission may be granted on ‘exceptional occasions… for development that would not normally be permitted on the site…because of who would benefit from the permission’81. As indicated above, if a grant of permission is justified in whole or part because of personal need and circumstances, the permission should be subject to a personal condition which names the beneficiaries and refers to their dependants.

250. Those named in the condition need not be restricted to or even include the appellant. The condition should list the names of the leading members of each family or group per pitch; where the leading members are an adult couple, their names should be separated by an ‘and/or’ (eg, Henry and/or Mary Smith) to take account of possible family breakdown or death.

251. The condition should refer to the ‘dependants’ of the leading members of the family group – but not name them in case, for example, more children are born. The implication of using the term dependant is that when and if those people are no longer dependant on the named individuals, or when those named are no longer resident, the continued occupation of the site by the one-time dependants is in breach of that condition.

252. A personal condition should apply for the lifetime of the beneficiaries but may be adapted so that it can be imposed alongside a temporary condition.

[^78]: Bromley LBC v SSCLG & Friend [2008] EWHC 3145 (Admin)

[^79]: Linfoot v SSCLG & Chorley BC [2012] EWHC 3514 (Admin)

[^80]: PPG paragraph 21a-014-20140306

[^81]: PPG paragraph 21a-015-20140306

<!-- Part2 p.165 -->

However, personal conditions are time-limited in any event because the named beneficiaries may move or will eventually die.

253. It follows that personal and/or temporary conditions should be worded to ensure that the use is ceased and the land restored to its previous condition in accordance with a scheme to be submitted and agreed at the end of the relevant period. This is so that the authority can enforce against any continued use of the land in breach of the temporary or personal condition.

254. The condition should include an early timetable for the submission of the restoration scheme, when the previous state of the land can be more easily established, the site occupants are present and there is a clear incentive for them to avoid the potentially serious consequences of not complying with the condition. The submission of a scheme at the end of time-limited condition is less likely, and moreover a scheme that is approved early will be enforceable against any subsequent owners of the land.

255. When considering a grant temporary or personal permission, the Inspector will need to address what other conditions would be necessary and reasonable given the scale and nature of any works that might be required and the duration of the permission. For example:

- If highway safety concerns could only be overcome through significant alterations to the site access, consider whether it would be reasonable to impose the burden of the works on the appellant when the duration of the permission would be short – and if not, whether temporary permission should be granted at all.

- If harm to the character of the area would be mitigated but not overcome by landscaping, and it would not be reasonable to impose the burden of the works on the appellant when the duration of the permission would be short, consider whether the condition is necessary at all, bearing in mind that the shorter duration of the permission will also mitigate harm.

256. The PPG states that imposing conditions on planning permissions for a change of use so as to require the demolition of buildings are unlikely to relate fairly and reasonably to the development permitted82. It may be necessary to canvas with the parties what elements of the proposed development should be permitted and/or required by condition in the event that the decision is to grant temporary and/or personal permission:

- Whether day or utility rooms could be provided in temporary structures.

- Whether hardstanding could be required to be removed.

- What drainage facilities and/or boundary treatments would be required.

82 PPG paragraph 21a-014-20140306

<!-- Part2 p.166 -->

## Other Conditions

257. PPTS paragraph 28 expects LPAs – and, by extension, Inspectors – to consider how they could overcome planning objections to particular proposal using planning conditions or obligations. However, this chapter does not duplicate advice in the Conditions ITM.

258. The PINS suite of suggested conditions includes model conditions for Traveller sites but, as in any other decision, the starting point should be the conditions suggested by the parties, and reasons should be given for imposing (or not) any condition.

259. In most cases, permission is granted for Traveller sites based on the special accommodation needs of Travellers. A condition should thus limit occupancy to Gypsies and Travellers (or Travelling Showpeople) as defined in PPTS 2024 or any subsequent replacement guidance. This condition may be imposed alongside a temporary or personal condition, with care taken to not exclude any relevant occupiers, including dependents, who have never travelled.

260. Since the grant of permission will generally be for the use of the land as a residential caravan site, it is usually necessary to impose a condition specifying the maximum number of caravans overall or the maximum number of pitches together with maximum number of caravans per pitch. The condition may also need to specify the types of caravan allowed; typically there will be a minimum of one static caravan and one touring caravan per pitch.

261. Since caravans may be moved by definition, a condition should be imposed to control the position of caravans within the site if that is necessary, perhaps for visual reasons. The condition should either tie the permission to the approved plans or require that details of the site layout are submitted to the Council for approval and then implemented as approved. Site licensing regulations require minimum distances between caravans for reasons of fire safety.

262. In accordance with PPTS paragraph 28b), however, another condition could specify a number of days per year when the site can be occupied by more than the allowed number of caravans, to allow for visitors or attendance at family or community events.

263. Amenity or toilet blocks, and day or utility rooms may also be required for site licensing reasons, as well as to meet the appellant’s own needs. If these are needed but not shown on submitted plans, a condition may again need to be imposed which requires the submission and approval of details.

264. Other matters which often need to be controlled by condition for Traveller sites, including through the submission of further details include:

- Hard and/or soft landscaping

- Boundary treatments

<!-- Part2 p.167 -->

- External illumination

- The means of access into the site

- The layout and surfacing of parking and turning areas

- Foul and surface water drainage, including sustainable drainage.

265. Travellers are less likely than in the past to need space for business activities and, if planning permission is sought strictly for residential use, bear in mind that conditions restricting business activities would not normally be considered reasonable or necessary in respect of any other residential development. The Council has powers in any event to enforce against any future unauthorised material change of use to put the site into commercial or mixed residential and commercial use.

266. However, where it is proposed to create a mixed use site – such as for Travelling Showpeople – or it is made clear that occupiers might need space for incidental (and acceptable) work-related activities, PPTS paragraph 28a) advises that conditions can limit which parts of a site are used for any business operation in order to minimise the visual impact and limit the effect on noise. As with any commercial use, conditions can also be imposed to control, for example, the height and/or nature of outdoor storage, hours of operation and/or harmful effects such as odour.

267. Travellers often own vehicles larger than domestic scale, for towing a caravan, transporting horses or working away. It is customary to impose a condition which limits the weight of vehicles and the number of large vehicles that may be parked or stored on a Traveller site. The usual upper weight limit is 3.5 tonnes, but sometimes a higher upper limit of 7.5 tonnes is accepted depending on the occupiers’ needs and any concerns regarding character and appearance, living conditions and/or highway safety.

268. When planning permission is to be granted for a transit site or transit pitches on a permanent site, conditions must be imposed to specify the length of time any occupier may reside on the site (as set out in PPTS paragraph 28c)) and the interval before which they may be permitted to return, and how such occupation is to be monitored by the local planning authority.

<!-- Part2 p.168 -->
